1. Why online learning: the freshness argument and its limits

1.1 The canonical evidence

Facebook ads (He et al., ADKDD 2014). The paper combined boosted decision trees as feature transforms with a logistic-regression head [2]. It measured how prediction quality decays as the gap between training data and serving day grows. Normalized entropy (NE) gets steadily worse with staleness. This motivated retraining the trees on a daily-or-slower cadence and training the linear head online on a real-time stream [2]. The paper also puts freshness in perspective. The largest wins came from the right features (historical features dominate) and the right model class. Freshness, learning-rate schedules and data sampling gave smaller gains [2]. The paper found per-coordinate learning rates to work best for the online head [2].

Google search ads (McMahan et al., KDD 2013). "Ad Click Prediction: a View from the Trenches" describes a logistic-regression model trained with FTRL-Proximal on a massive stream. It uses per-coordinate learning rates, L1-induced sparsity, probabilistic feature admission (Poisson or Bloom-filter inclusion), 16-bit fixed-point weights, calibration layers and extensive monitoring [1]. Its memory techniques reappear almost unchanged in 2020s embedding systems as frequency filters, expiry and quantized embedding storage. Monolith's code carries occurrence_threshold, probabilistic and sliding-window hash filters, and a quantized entry accessor [4].

ByteDance (Monolith, 2022). The Monolith paper argues that general-purpose frameworks "separate batch training and serving completely". That separation stops a model from reacting to user feedback in real time, and the paper shows serving AUC improving as the training-to-serving sync interval shrinks [3].

1.2 Stages of maturity

Chip Huyen's progression is a useful vocabulary [36]:

  • stage 1: manual, stateless retraining from scratch;
  • stage 2: automated retraining on a schedule;
  • stage 3: automated stateful training, where each run fine-tunes from the previous checkpoint on new data;
  • stage 4: continual learning, where updates are triggered by data or performance signals rather than the calendar.

She identifies the main obstacles as access to fresh labels, evaluating every update and algorithms suited to incremental updates [36]. Google's MLOps guidance calls the stage-2 and stage-3 capability "continuous training" (CT). Its triggers are schedule, new-data arrival or drift alerts, and it is gated by automated data and model validation [37].

2. Streaming training for recommendation: ByteDance Monolith

2.1 Problem

Short-video and ads recommendation at ByteDance faces two problems that batch frameworks handle badly [3]:

  1. Sparse, dynamic ID spaces. User IDs, item IDs and their crosses arrive continuously. Most appear rarely, and many go stale. Hashing them into a fixed-size table causes collisions that hurt quality.
  2. Concept drift. User interests and trending content change within hours. A model refreshed daily misses "hotspots", which the repository README describes as the motivation for real-time training [4].

2.2 Architecture

  user actions (clicks, plays, likes)            features at serve time
              |                                         |
              v                                         v
        Kafka: action queue                     Kafka: feature queue
              \                                        /
               \                                      /
                v                                    v
         +--------------------------------------------------+
         |  JOINER (Flink)                                  |
         |  key = unique request id                         |
         |  in-memory cache + on-disk KV for features whose |
         |  actions have not arrived yet                    |
         |  negative sampling applied here                  |
         +--------------------------------------------------+
                              |
                              v
                 Kafka: joined training examples ----> also dumped to HDFS
                              |                         (batch training / replay)
                              v
         +-----------------------------------------+
         |  ONLINE TRAINING                        |
         |  workers <-> training PS                |
         |  - collisionless cuckoo-hash embeddings |
         |  - occurrence filter, expiry            |
         |  - touched-key set (ids since last sync)|
         +-----------------------------------------+
               | sparse: only touched keys,     | dense: full, on a
               | minute-level cadence           | slower cadence
               v                                v
         +-----------------------------------------+
         |  SERVING PS (embedding KV)  <- entry    |
         |  servers run the dense graph and call   |
         |  PS for embeddings                      |
         +-----------------------------------------+

The data flow above follows the paper [3]. The serving split is visible in the repository: Monolith exports two kinds of TensorFlow SavedModel, an entry that receives client calls and runs the dense graph, and one or more PS shards that act as embedding key-value stores. Only the entry calls the PS [4].

2.3 Key techniques

  • Collisionless embedding table. Monolith uses a cuckoo hash map, with two tables and two hash functions. An insert that finds its slot taken evicts the occupant to its alternate table, so distinct IDs never share an embedding [3]. The repository implements this in runtime/hash_table/cuckoohash/ [4].
  • Bounding memory without collisions. Two mechanisms keep the table bounded. Frequency filtering means an ID is admitted only after it has been seen a configurable number of times (occurrence_threshold per feature slot). It is implemented with probabilistic and sliding-window hash filters. Expirable embeddings means each entry carries a last-update timestamp, and an ID untouched for longer than its slot's expire_time is evicted [3][4]. Expiry is deliberate forgetting: it trades memory, and some long-tail knowledge, for capacity to learn new IDs.
  • Incremental parameter sync. Most bytes are in sparse embeddings, but only a small fraction of IDs are updated in any short window. The training PS therefore tracks the set of IDs trained since the last sync (the touched keys), and at sync time pushes only those keys' embeddings to the serving PS. Dense parameters move slowly and are synced less often [3]. In the open-source code, each ParameterSyncClient owns a single concurrent hopscotch hash set of (key, table) pairs that every attached hash table writes into. Its capacity is the constant MAX_TOUCHED_KEYS = 64 * 1024 * 1024 / (8 * 4), about 2.1 million entries, and the sync step drains it with GetAndClear() [4].
  • Negative sampling with correction. Negatives are subsampled in the joiner. The paper applies log-odds correction at serving so predicted probabilities stay calibrated, the same issue Facebook solved with re-calibration [2][3].
  • Streaming input. Training reads directly from Kafka. The tutorial's create_plain_kafka_dataset treats the poll batch size as the effective training batch size [4].

2.4 Reported results

  • Collisionless vs. collision tables. On public data, and in production, collisionless tables improved AUC over hashed tables with collisions [3].
  • Sync interval. In an experiment that simulated online training on a public CTR dataset with sync intervals of 5 hours, 1 hour and 30 minutes, AUC improved as the interval shrank. In production A/B tests, real-time training improved over batch training (exact deltas: see [3]; approximately tenths of an AUC point).
  • Fault tolerance vs. freshness. The paper deliberately trades reliability for real-time learning. Because a PS failure loses only that shard's recent updates, it compared hourly and daily PS snapshots and found only a negligible AUC difference. It concluded that daily snapshots are acceptable and cheaper [3].

2.5 Failure modes and lessons

  • Joiner backlog. If the action stream lags, features accumulate in the on-disk KV store and examples arrive late. Training on partially joined data biases labels toward negative (compare Section 3).
  • Eviction policy is a model hyperparameter. Expiry and admission thresholds change what the model can remember. They need offline sweeps like any regularizer.
  • Freshness beats durability, but only for recoverable state. Monolith's snapshot argument works because a lost shard is relearned quickly from the stream. Systems with slowly learned state, such as dense towers or long-tail embeddings, cannot make the same trade so cheaply.

3. Delayed feedback: the joiner is the learning algorithm

Online training needs labels, and labels arrive late. A click can come seconds after an impression, and a conversion can come days later. How the system decides that a non-event is a negative directly biases the model.

3.1 Facebook's online joiner (2014)

Facebook's online data joiner pairs impressions with clicks inside a waiting window [2]. The window trades label correctness against freshness and memory. If it is too short, late clicks are missed and empirical CTR is biased low. If it is too long, buffering costs grow and training lags. The paper also warns that if the click stream stalls, the joiner will emit only negatives, and an online trainer will learn that nobody clicks. It recommends protection mechanisms that disconnect the online trainer from the joiner when the real-time training distribution shifts abruptly [2]. This is an early published example of a closed-loop circuit breaker.

3.2 Twitter: fake negatives in continuous training (2019)

Ktena et al. describe continuous training of ads CTR models at Twitter [5]. Every impression is ingested immediately as a negative. If an engagement later arrives, a positive copy is ingested too, so some negatives are "fake negatives". The paper compares loss formulations that correct for this. Fake-negative weighting and fake-negative calibration are derived from the joint distribution of observed and true labels, alongside importance-weighting baselines. The paper reports that the corrected losses beat naive training both offline and in online experiments [5]. The design avoids a waiting window entirely. Freshness is maximal, and the bias is corrected in the loss.

3.3 Conversion delays: Alibaba ES-DFM (2021)

For conversion-rate prediction, Yang et al. propose elapsed-time sampling. An example is held for a short elapsed window before it is emitted. The model then importance-weights between the observed and true label distributions to correct the remaining fake negatives [38]. Chapelle's 2014 delayed-feedback model, which jointly models conversion probability and delay distribution, is the common ancestor of this line [39].

  impression t0 ----------------------------------------------------> time
       |          click at t0+20s              conversion at t0+3d
       |               |                              |
  Facebook (wait W):  [==== W ====] emit (pos/neg)    (missed if > W)
  Twitter (FN):       emit NEG at t0 | emit POS copy at click | loss corrects
  ES-DFM:             [= e =] emit; importance weights for later conversions
  Monolith:           Flink join by request id; on-disk KV holds unjoined features

4. Moving parameters: dissemination, checkpointing and state

Online training is only useful if updated parameters reach serving quickly and safely, and if the large mutable state can be recovered after a failure.

4.1 Ekko: low-latency model updates (Tencent and Edinburgh, OSDI 2022)

Ekko targets the update path for very large deep-learning recommendation models (DLRMs) served from geo-distributed data centers [6]. Its three components are:

  1. Peer-to-peer update dissemination. Synchronizing parameters in place, instead of shipping full model files, exploits the sparsity and temporal locality of updates.
  2. An SLO-aware update scheduler. It prioritizes updates that matter most for model quality when bandwidth is constrained.
  3. A model-state manager. It watches serving SLOs and rolls back updates that harm quality.

The paper reports update latencies on the order of seconds for multi-terabyte models, orders of magnitude below file-based pipelines (approximate) [6]. The design point is that an online-learning system needs an update-level rollback, not only a model-version rollback.

4.2 Check-N-Run: checkpointing mutable embeddings (Meta, NSDI 2022)

Recommendation training jobs run for long periods on massive embedding tables, so checkpoint write bandwidth and storage become bottlenecks. Check-N-Run uses two levers [7]. Differential checkpointing writes only the embedding rows modified since the last checkpoint, the same "touched keys" insight as Monolith's sync. Quantization compresses checkpoints. The paper reports large reductions in write bandwidth and storage capacity (approximately 6-17x and 2.5-8x respectively, as reported) [7].

4.3 PERSIA and dynamic-embedding stacks

PERSIA, from Kuaishou and ETH Zurich, uses hybrid synchronization. Dense layers train synchronously on GPUs, while embeddings update asynchronously on a CPU parameter server [8]. Its README cites training up to 100 trillion parameters and production validation "with 100 million level DAU at Kuaishou" [8]. The project is marked unmaintained after a company reorganization [8], a reminder that open-source online-training stacks often outlive their sponsors. TensorFlow Recommenders-Addons (TFRA) covers similar ground for the TensorFlow ecosystem. Its README centers on trainable, resizable dynamic embeddings backed by pluggable key-value stores (a CPU cuckoo hash map, NVIDIA's GPU HierarchicalKV, or Redis), and on "half synchronous" Horovod training that is synchronous for dense weights and asynchronous for sparse ones [40]. The design RFC behind it names online learning as the motivation: tracking user interests in real time "requires eliminating and adding weights on running-time without frequently restart training" [40].

4.4 Lessons

  • The sparse/dense asymmetry recurs everywhere. Sparse rows change fast and locally, while dense weights change slowly and globally. Monolith's sync [3], Check-N-Run's checkpoints [7], PERSIA's hybrid synchronization [8] and TFRA's half-synchronous mode [40] all exploit it.
  • Update validation has to be continuous. Ekko's rollback [6] and Facebook's joiner circuit breaker [2] are two of the few published guardrails that act at the update level rather than the release level.

5. Bandit loops: learning the policy, not just the predictor

A streaming CTR model learns from whatever the current policy chose to show. A bandit system designs the data it learns from. It explores, logs the probability of each action and updates the policy online. Chapter 01 covers the degenerate feedback loops that motivate this. Without exploration, even an accurate model narrows coverage [41].

5.1 Yahoo! LinUCB (2010) and replay evaluation (2011)

Li et al. framed news-article recommendation on the Yahoo! Today module as a contextual bandit. LinUCB keeps a ridge-regression estimate per arm and picks the arm with the highest upper confidence bound [9]. On logged Yahoo traffic, LinUCB achieved a 12.5% click lift over a standard context-free bandit [9]. The companion WSDM 2011 paper showed that if logs are collected with a uniformly random policy, replay, which keeps only events where the candidate policy agrees with the logged action, gives an unbiased offline estimate of a new policy's online CTR [10]. This made bandit iteration possible without live experiments for every variant.

5.2 Microsoft Decision Service and MSN (2016-2017)

Agarwal et al. present the Decision Service (the paper's later arXiv versions are titled "Making Contextual Decisions with Low Technical Debt") as a general-purpose system for contextual-bandit learning. It is built from four abstractions connected in a loop, explore, log, learn and deploy. Exploration and logging are designed so that the logged data is correct and unbiased, which lets the learner train online, supports real-time safeguards and keeps every decision reproducible [11]. The reported production deployments include content-recommendation services with click-through improvements in the 25-30% range and a landing page with an 18% revenue lift (as reported) [11]. Agarwal and Langford's Microsoft Research blog reports that clicks on MSN.com rose 26% after a contextual-bandit system went live in January 2016. The same technology shipped as the Custom Decision Service in Azure Cognitive Services, as open source on GitHub, and as algorithms in Vowpal Wabbit [12]. The project page describes Multiworld Testing as evaluating K policies with data and computation that scale logarithmically in K, unlike A/B testing [13].

            +-----------+    context x     +--------------------+
  request ->|  EXPLORE  |----------------->|  policy pi_t       |
            | (eps-grdy,|<-- action a,  ---|  (VW learner)      |
            |  bagging, |    p(a|x)        +--------------------+
            |  softmax) |                           ^
            +-----------+                           | deploy new pi_{t+1}
                  | (x, a, p)                       | (minutes)
                  v                                 |
            +-----------+  join reward r  +---------+----------+
            |   LOG     |---------------->|   LEARN (online)   |
            | (x,a,p,r) |                 |   + off-policy eval|
            +-----------+                 |   (IPS / DR) for   |
                                          |   safeguards       |
                                          +--------------------+

5.3 Netflix artwork personalization (2017)

Netflix chooses which artwork to show each member for each title using contextual bandits [14]. Regret from exploration is accepted as the price of learning. Impressions are logged with the selection probability, and new policies are evaluated offline with a replay metric over the explored data before online A/B tests [14]. The design point for system builders is that the logging schema, including the propensity, is the contract between serving and learning.

5.4 Off-policy correction at YouTube scale (2019)

Chen et al. treat YouTube recommendation as a REINFORCE policy learned from logs produced by many earlier policies. They correct with importance weights, a top-K correction for slates, and variance-control techniques [42]. This is the batch, large-action-space counterpart to online bandits. The loop closes on the training cadence rather than per event, but the propensity discipline is the same.

5.5 Open Bandit Dataset and Pipeline: a public testbed for the offline gate (ZOZO, 2021)

Most bandit logs stay private, so the off-policy evaluation (OPE) step that gates every new policy is rarely tested against ground truth. The Open Bandit Dataset fixes that for one real system. ZOZO logged its ZOZOTOWN fashion e-commerce recommender over a 7-day experiment on three campaigns (all, men's and women's items), with three recommendation positions per page. Each campaign randomly served either a uniform-random policy or Bernoulli Thompson sampling [45]. Because two different policies ran on the same platform and traffic, one policy's logs can be used to estimate the other's value, and the estimate can be checked against that policy's actual on-policy outcome. This is the replay idea of [10] turned into a benchmark for OPE estimators. The companion Open Bandit Pipeline is a Python package that standardizes preprocessing, off-policy learning and OPE estimators (DM, IPW, self-normalized IPW, DR and more robust DR variants) behind one interface [45]. For system builders the lesson is practical. Before trusting an IPS or DR gate in a production bandit loop, validate it on data where the answer is known, ideally by keeping a small slice of traffic on a logged randomized policy, as ZOZO did.

5.6 Lessons

  • Exploration is infrastructure. The Decision Service shows that exploration, propensity logging and offline evaluation work best as shared platform features, not as per-team code [11].
  • Online learning amplifies whatever the reward measures. Fast bandit updates on click rewards converge quickly to click-optimal and possibly engagement-bait policies. The guardrails must be as fast as the learner.

6. Catastrophic forgetting: the cost of learning in sequence

6.1 The phenomenon and classic mitigations

When a network is trained sequentially on shifting data, gradient updates for the new distribution overwrite parameters that encoded the old one. Three families of mitigation dominate.

  • Regularization. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) adds a quadratic penalty that anchors each parameter to its old value, weighted by the diagonal Fisher information, so weights important for earlier tasks move less [15]. It was demonstrated on sequential MNIST permutations and sequential Atari games [15].
  • Replay and constrained optimization. Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM) keeps a small episodic memory per task. It projects each new gradient so that it does not increase loss on the stored examples [16]. Plain experience replay, which mixes old data into new batches, is the simplest and most widely used baseline in production.
  • Architecture. This family isolates or grows parameters per task.

Van de Ven, Tuytelaars and Tolias distinguish three continual-learning scenarios: task-incremental, domain-incremental and class-incremental. They show that methods that look strong in one scenario can fail in another. Class-incremental learning, where the task identity is never given, is hardest, and replay-based methods are generally needed there [43].

6.2 Forgetting in production recommenders is often wanted

Recommendation streams are non-stationary by design. Monolith's expiry and the forgetting implicit in a high learning rate on fresh data are features, not bugs [3]. The production question is what to forget. Stale item embeddings and dead trends should go. Stable user preferences, rare-but-valuable segments, and the calibration of the dense tower should stay. Separating fast-changing sparse state from slow-changing dense state (Section 4.4) is the systems-level answer. It amounts to a parameter-level learning-rate split.

6.3 LLM-era findings

  • LoRA learns less and forgets less (Biderman et al., 2024). For continued pretraining and instruction fine-tuning on code and math, LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning on the target domain but better preserves source-domain abilities. The weight perturbations that full fine-tuning learns have far higher rank than typical LoRA configurations (reported 10-100x) [17]. Parameter-efficient updates act as an implicit regularizer against forgetting, at the cost of plasticity.
  • ...but for RL, LoRA's plasticity cost largely disappears ("LoRA Without Regret", Schulman et al., Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). The post reports that LoRA matches full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL even at rank 1. The argument is information-theoretic: an episode's scalar advantage carries only about O(1) bits, so a tiny adapter has enough capacity to absorb it [46]. Read together with [17] and [18], this suggests a cheap default for closed-loop LLM updates, namely low-rank adapters trained on-policy. It also has a systems payoff, covered in Section 9.3: a rank-1 adapter is megabytes, not gigabytes, so it can be shipped to serving as a delta [53].
  • On-policy RL forgets less than SFT ("RL's Razor", Shenfeld, Pari and Agrawal, 2025). At matched performance on a new task, RL fine-tuning preserves prior capabilities better than supervised fine-tuning. The amount of forgetting is predicted by the KL divergence between the fine-tuned and base policies, measured on the new task's distribution. On-policy RL is implicitly biased toward KL-minimal solutions among those that solve the task [18]. For closed-loop LLM products, this argues for on-policy updates, such as Cursor's online RL [34], over repeated SFT on logged data when retaining general capability matters.
  • Sparse memory fine-tuning (Lin et al., Meta FAIR, 2025). This builds on memory layers, which add a large key-value memory sparsely accessed per token [20]. New facts are learned by updating only the memory slots that the new data activates far more than pretraining data did, ranked with a TF-IDF-style score [19]. In the reported fact-learning experiment, held-out NaturalQuestions performance dropped about 89% with full fine-tuning and about 71% with LoRA, against about 11% with sparse memory fine-tuning, at comparable new-knowledge acquisition (approximate, as reported) [19]. The architectural lesson is that sparse, addressable parameters make continual updates local. The same property makes Monolith's per-ID embeddings safe to update every minute.

6.4 On-policy learning from demonstrations: self-distillation fine-tuning (2026)

RL's Razor [18] leaves a gap. On-policy RL forgets less, but it needs a reward function, and many production updates arrive as demonstrations, such as corrected outputs, new documents or tool traces, which normally feed off-policy SFT. Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT; Shenfeld et al., ICML 2026) closes that gap with in-context learning [47]. The same model, conditioned on a demonstration, acts as the teacher. The unconditioned model samples its own outputs, and the training signal is the divergence between the student's and the demonstration-conditioned teacher's token distributions on those on-policy samples. The authors report that SDFT beats SFT on skill-learning and knowledge-acquisition tasks, with higher new-task accuracy and substantially less forgetting, and that one model can accumulate several skills sequentially without regression [47].

Two caveats belong next to the claim. First, the authors later found that all of the paper's results came from a per-token forward-KL loss, not the reverse KL analyzed in the paper's theory. The repository default was changed and the arXiv version clarified [47][48]. Second, an independent reproduction during Hugging Face's ICML 2026 agent-reproduction challenge did not reproduce the headline gain of about 4 points with the authors' own code and data [48]. The design idea, turning demonstrations into an on-policy signal so that updates stay close to the current policy, is sound and consistent with [18]. The magnitude of the benefit should be treated as unsettled.

7. Continual pretraining of LLMs

7.1 Problem

Pretraining a frontier model from scratch for every new data snapshot is prohibitively expensive. Continual pretraining (CPT) instead resumes from a checkpoint on new data, such as newer crawls, a new language or a new domain. It must avoid two failures: losing old capabilities, and failing to absorb the new distribution because the learning rate has already decayed.

7.2 Re-warming and the stability gap

Gupta et al. ("How to (re)warm your model?", 2023) studied resuming Pythia-style models on a new corpus [21]. Re-warming the learning rate initially increases loss on both upstream and downstream data. Over longer training, however, re-warming and re-decaying improves downstream performance compared with continuing at a small learning rate. The exact warmup length matters less [21].

Guo et al. (2024) named the transient dip the stability gap: performance on target-domain tasks first drops and only later recovers when CPT starts [23]. They propose efficient strategies against it. These are multiple epochs over a smaller subset, training on a high-quality subset first, and a data mixture similar to the pretraining distribution, demonstrated on medical-domain CPT of Llama-3-8B [23][25].

7.3 Simple and scalable strategies (Ibrahim et al., 2024)

Ibrahim et al. show that a simple recipe matches retraining from scratch on the union of old and new data [22]:

  • re-warm the learning rate;
  • re-decay it;
  • replay a fraction of the previous data.

They test at 405M and 10B parameters, under a weak shift (Pile to SlimPajama) and a strong shift (English to German) [22]. The replay fraction needed grows with shift strength (reported at about 5% for the weak shift and substantially more for the language shift; approximate). The authors also propose "infinite" learning-rate schedules that avoid repeated re-warming by keeping a constant phase from which annealed checkpoints are branched [22].

7.4 Time-continual benchmarks (Apple TiC-LM, 2025)

TiC-LM builds a web-scale time-continual pretraining benchmark from successive Common Crawl dumps (TiC-CC). Time-stratified evaluations come from Wikipedia, StackExchange and code documentation (TiC-Wiki, TiC-StackExchange, TiC-CodeDocs) [24]. The repository ships code for the continual-learning methods benchmarked and for "Oracle" models retrained from scratch [24]. The paper reports that schedule-plus-replay strategies can approach Oracle retraining at a fraction of the compute. It also reports that the best replay ratio depends on the domain: general web knowledge benefits from replay, while fast-changing domains such as code documentation benefit less (summary, approximate) [24].

7.5 Design pattern

  checkpoint C_k (annealed, deployed)
        |
        +-- branch from constant-LR "trunk" (infinite schedule) or re-warm from C_k
        |
        v
  data_mix = new_shard (1 - r)  +  replay of old corpora (r)   r ~ shift strength
        |
        v
  re-warm LR -> constant -> re-decay      monitor: old-domain evals (forgetting),
        |                                 new-domain evals (plasticity), stability gap
        v
  C_{k+1}  --> alignment/RL refresh --> eval gates --> deploy

The open problem is that the post-training stack, including SFT, RLHF and safety tuning, sits on top of the pretrained checkpoint. CPT can erode aligned behavior. Li and Lee examine forgetting when an already-aligned chat model is continually pretrained, measuring losses in output format, knowledge and reliability [51], and the survey literature catalogs the wider problem [25]. In practice, many teams re-run post-training after every CPT step.

8. Test-time training: closing the loop inside a request

TTT methods update some parameters on the test input itself, using a self-supervised or task-derived objective, before or while producing the output. Where online learning closes the loop over users, TTT closes it within the request.

8.1 Distribution shift: TTT (2019) and TENT (2021)

  • TTT with self-supervision (Sun et al., ICML 2020). A shared feature extractor feeds both the main classifier and an auxiliary self-supervised head that predicts image rotation. At test time, the shared encoder takes gradient steps on the rotation loss for the single test image, or keeps updating across an online stream. This improves robustness on corrupted and shifted benchmarks such as CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-10.1 [26].
  • TENT (Wang, Shelhamer et al., ICLR 2021). This is fully test-time adaptation. It needs no auxiliary training: it minimizes prediction entropy on test batches and updates only normalization statistics and affine parameters, with "just one update per batch to not interrupt inference" [27]. In the repository's illustrative CIFAR-10-C example (WRN-28-10, severity 5), mean error falls from 43.5% (source model) to 20.4% (test-time normalization only) to 18.6% (TENT) [27]. Most of the gain comes from re-estimating normalization statistics. This is a cheap, robust production trick, while entropy minimization adds a smaller increment and a risk of collapse on long non-stationary streams.

8.2 TTT as architecture: TTT layers, Titans and Nested Learning

  • TTT layers (Sun et al., 2024). The recurrent hidden state is a model, either a linear model (TTT-Linear) or a two-layer MLP (TTT-MLP). The state update rule is a step of self-supervised learning on the incoming tokens, so the layer literally trains on the test sequence [28]. The authors pitch this as linear-complexity sequence modeling with a more expressive state than classic RNNs. They provide JAX training code, PyTorch inference code and dedicated kernels [28].
  • Titans (Behrouz, Zhong and Mirrokni, Google, 2025). Titans adds a neural long-term memory, an MLP whose weights are updated at test time. The update is driven by a "surprise" signal, the gradient of an associative-memory loss, with momentum and a learned forgetting (weight-decay) gate. The memory is combined with attention as short-term memory in three variants: memory as context, as gate, or as layer [29]. The paper reports scaling to context windows beyond 2M tokens, with strong needle-in-haystack results (reported) [29]. An unofficial PyTorch implementation exposes the memory module as a drop-in NeuralMemory with configurable chunk size [44].
  • Nested Learning and Hope (Google, NeurIPS 2025). The same group generalizes the idea by treating a model as a set of nested optimization problems, each updated at its own frequency. Optimizers and attention are viewed as associative memories within this framing. Their proof-of-concept architecture, Hope, is a self-modifying variant of Titans paired with a "continuum memory system", a spectrum of MLP blocks updated at different rates. Google presents it explicitly as a continual-learning architecture and reports lower perplexity and better long-context recall than Titans and other recurrent baselines (as reported) [52]. For this chapter, the significance is conceptual. The fast and slow state split that recommender engineers implement in infrastructure (Section 4.4) becomes a multi-timescale update schedule inside the network.
  • TTT for long video (CVPR 2025). TTT-MLP layers are added to a pretrained CogVideoX 5B diffusion transformer. The original attention handles each 3-second segment locally, and TTT layers process the global sequence and its reverse, gated residually. Context is extended in stages to 9, 18, 30 and 63 seconds, and the authors' custom TTT-MLP kernel targets H100s [31].

The engineering consequence of these designs is that "online learning" moves from the MLOps layer into the kernel. Update rules, learning rates and forgetting gates become architecture hyperparameters, and per-request state is weights rather than a KV cache.

8.3 TTT for reasoning: ARC (Akyürek et al., 2024)

Akyürek, Damani, Qiu, Guo, Kim and Andreas show that per-task test-time training substantially lifts abstract-reasoning accuracy [30]. For each ARC task, they build a small training set from the task's own demonstrations, using leave-one-out sub-tasks plus geometric augmentations. They train a task-specific LoRA adapter on a fine-tuned Llama-3-class 8B model and predict with augmented inference plus voting. The reference configuration in the repository uses LoRA rank 128, alpha 16, learning rate 5e-5, 2 epochs and batch size 2 [30]. The paper reports up to about a 6x accuracy improvement over the fine-tuned baseline without TTT, and 53% on the ARC public validation set with an 8B model. Ensembled with program-synthesis methods, it reaches about 61.9%, comparable to the average human score (as reported) [30].

Cost profile: every task pays for a LoRA training run at inference time. TTT therefore trades latency and GPU-seconds for accuracy, and fits batch or offline reasoning workloads better than interactive serving.

8.4 Self-editing models: SEAL (MIT, 2025) and hypernetwork adapters

SEAL (Self-Adapting LLMs) trains a model with RL to generate its own self-edits: fine-tuning data and update directives, such as augmentations and hyperparameters, written in response to new input. The resulting weight update's downstream performance serves as the reward [32]. It is explored in two settings, incorporating new factual knowledge and adapting to new tasks from few-shot examples. Experiments run on two A100 or H100 GPUs [32]. The paper reports that RL-trained self-edits beat both training on raw passages and training on synthetic data from a much larger model for knowledge incorporation. It also reports large gains over in-context learning on a curated ARC subset (approximate) [32]. The authors flag catastrophic forgetting under repeated sequential self-edits, and the per-edit cost of an inner fine-tune plus evaluation, as limitations [32].

Sakana AI's Text-to-LoRA is the amortized alternative. A hypernetwork generates a task-specific LoRA adapter from a natural-language task description in a single forward pass, avoiding per-task gradient descent at adaptation time [33].

  TTT DESIGN SPACE
                       what is updated           objective at test time   cost/request
  TENT                 norm stats + affine       entropy                  1 step/batch
  TTT (2019)           shared encoder            rotation prediction      k steps
  TTT layers / Titans  per-sequence fast weights self-supervised recon.   O(tokens)
  ARC TTT              per-task LoRA             leave-one-out demos      full LoRA run
  SEAL                 LoRA/full via self-edit   model-written data (RL)  inner finetune

8.5 Test-time reinforcement learning: TTRL (2025)

TTRL (Zuo et al., Tsinghua and Shanghai AI Lab, NeurIPS 2025) asks whether a reasoning model can run RL on unlabeled test questions [49]. The missing reward is estimated with a standard test-time-scaling trick. The model samples many answers per question, the majority answer is treated as a pseudo-label, and each sample is rewarded for agreeing with it. The repository reports that this boosts Qwen2.5-Math-7B's pass@1 on AIME 2024 by about 211% using only unlabeled test data. It also reports that the trained model surpasses the initial model's own maj@n, the nominal ceiling of its supervision, and approaches models trained on the test data with ground-truth labels [49]. TTRL has since been folded into the verl RL framework behind a single flag [49].

For closed-loop design, TTRL is the batch-RL counterpart of per-task TTT (Section 8.3). It closes the loop over a distribution of incoming unlabeled queries rather than one request. Its risk is the same self-reinforcement that makes entropy-based TTA collapse (Section 8.1): if the majority is confidently wrong, the reward pushes the model further toward that answer. Deployments therefore need a held-out labeled slice to detect drift. The approach suits domains with verifiable or consensus-friendly answers, such as math and code, much better than open-ended generation.

9. Online learning from product signals in LLM systems

9.1 Cursor Tab: on-policy RL with frequent redeploys (2025)

Cursor reports that its Tab completion model serves over 400 million requests per day. It is trained with policy-gradient RL: positive reward for accepted suggestions, a penalty for rejected ones, and zero for staying silent [34]. Because the method is on-policy, Cursor redeploys checkpoints frequently throughout the day so that training data comes from the current policy. The new model makes 21% fewer suggestions with a 28% higher accept rate [34]. Deployment latency becomes a hyperparameter of the learning algorithm, the same lesson Monolith learned for CTR models [3]. RL's Razor [18] suggests that on-policy updates also keep forgetting low.

9.2 Cautionary case: GPT-4o sycophancy (2025)

OpenAI's postmortem describes an April 2025 update that added a reward signal based on ChatGPT thumbs-up and thumbs-down data. In aggregate, this weakened the primary reward signal that had been holding sycophancy in check. Offline evaluations did not catch the regression, and a full rollback took about 24 hours [35]. User-feedback loops optimize the proxy the users emit. The faster the update loop, the more the evaluation gate must test for the behaviors the proxy rewards by accident.

9.3 The LLM parameter server: weight sync and staleness in asynchronous RL (2025-2026)

Online RL on LLMs, whether from product signals like Cursor's or from verifiable rewards, has rebuilt the recommender stack of Sections 2 and 4 under new names. A March 2026 Hugging Face survey of 16 open-source RL libraries finds that all of them converged on the same architecture. Inference GPUs and training GPUs are physically separated, a buffer decouples them, and weights are pushed asynchronously from trainer to generators so that "generation never stops and training never waits" [50]. This is Monolith's training-PS/serving-PS split, with rollouts in place of joined click examples.

The survey identifies the same two design axes that recommender engineers face [50]:

  • Weight synchronization. Transports range from NCCL broadcast (roughly 100-500 ms) and bucketed NCCL (about 20 ms in verl) to CUDA IPC, filesystem plus HTTP, and filesystem plus restart. The interrupt model matters as much as the transport. PipelineRL swaps weights between individual decode steps, so in-flight sequences continue under the new policy. Other libraries abort in-flight requests, drain them, or block a whole batch.
  • Staleness management. Rollouts are generated under a policy several steps behind the trainer, so the data is off-policy, just as a CTR model trains on impressions chosen by its predecessor. Three orthogonal remedies appear. Version rejection tags each sample with its policy version and drops samples that are too old. Depth bounding caps the buffer so lag cannot exceed a limit. Importance-sampling correction reweights stale samples with clipped ratios. The production trend is hybrid: bounded queues plus optional truncated IS [50].

Low-rank adapters change the economics of the sync. Because rank-1 LoRA suffices for policy-gradient RL [46], a follow-up Hugging Face write-up ships only the adapter, a few megabytes for a 1.5B model against about 3 GB for full weights. It moves the adapter through shared storage instead of NCCL, and vLLM keeps several adapter versions loaded so that old rollouts finish under the policy they started with [53]. This is the LLM analogue of Monolith's touched-key sync and Ekko's delta dissemination (Sections 2.3 and 4.1): ship deltas, not models, and keep version identity attached to every sample.

11. Failure modes catalog

Failure mode Where it bites Symptom Published defenses
Label-stream outage Streaming CTR Predicted CTR collapses toward 0 Joiner circuit breaker [2]; distribution-shift alarms
Delayed-label bias Conversions, slow engagements Systematic under-prediction Waiting window [2], fake-negative losses [5], elapsed-time sampling [38], delay models [39]
Joiner backlog / skew Kafka + Flink pipelines Fresh model trained on stale or partial joins Request-id joins with on-disk spill [3]; lag SLOs
Embedding table blow-up Dynamic ID spaces OOM, latency spikes Frequency admission, expiry [1][3][4]
Harmful update reaches serving Any minute-level push Sudden quality or SLO regression Update-level rollback [6]; canary PS shards
Checkpoint cost / data loss Long-running online jobs Lost state after PS failure Differential + quantized checkpoints [7]; accept loss of recoverable state [3]
Degenerate loop Recommenders without exploration Coverage and novelty shrink Exploration budget and propensity logs [9][11][41]
Catastrophic forgetting Sequential fine-tuning, CPT Old-domain evals drop Replay [16][22], EWC [15], LoRA [17], on-policy RL [18], sparse memory [19]
Stability gap Start of CPT Transient drop on target tasks Subset multi-epoch training, high-quality data first [23]
Proxy-reward drift Online RL from user signals Sycophancy, reward hacking Targeted evals, reward balance, human launch gate [35]
TTT collapse Entropy-based adaptation, majority-vote test-time RL Confident wrong predictions over time Restrict updated params [27]; periodic reset; labeled hold-out slice for TTRL-style loops [49]
Untrustworthy offline gate Bandit and RL policy evaluation OPE ranks policies differently from online results Validate estimators on multi-policy logged data [45]; keep a randomized logging slice [10]
Rollout staleness Asynchronous LLM RL Training on samples from an outdated policy; instability Version rejection, bounded buffers, truncated IS [50]
Irreproducible continual-learning gains Adopting new forgetting mitigations Paper gains vanish in-house Re-run on own data; check loss matches paper [47][48]

Key takeaways for system designers

  1. Treat freshness as one input among several. Facebook found features and model class mattered more than freshness [2], while ByteDance measured clear gains from cutting sync intervals to minutes [3]. Measure the staleness curve (quality against training-serving gap) for your domain before building a streaming stack.
  2. Split fast and slow state. Sparse embeddings tolerate, and need, minute-level updates. Dense towers and tree feature transforms change slowly and anchor behavior. Sync, checkpoint and learning rates should follow that split [2][3][7][8].
  3. The joiner is part of the model. Waiting windows, fake-negative corrections and delay models determine label bias [2][5][38][39]. Version and test them like model code, and put a circuit breaker on label-stream health [2].
  4. Ship deltas, not models, and make deltas reversible. Touched-key sync [3][4], differential checkpoints [7] and update-level rollback [6] are the core primitives for minute-scale loops. Asynchronous LLM RL rediscovered the same primitives: separated trainer and generator pools, versioned samples, staleness bounds and adapter-only sync [50][53].
  5. Make exploration and propensity logging platform features. Bandit loops are only as good as their logs. Explore, log, learn and deploy should be infrastructure, with replay and off-policy evaluation as the offline gate [9][10][11][14]. Validate that gate itself on data where the true answer is known [45].
  6. Choose deliberately what the system forgets. Expiry and admission thresholds [3] are memory policy. For LLMs, prefer low-KL update paths, namely LoRA [17][46], on-policy RL [18], on-policy self-distillation when only demonstrations exist [47] and sparse memory updates [19], when general capability must be preserved. Keep replay data for every corpus you care about [22], and reproduce a mitigation's gains on your own data before relying on them [48].
  7. Plan continual pretraining as a schedule problem. Re-warm, re-decay and replay [21][22], or use infinite schedules with branchable annealed checkpoints [22]. Budget for the stability gap [23] and for re-running post-training.
  8. Treat test-time training as a compute dial. Normalization re-estimation and TENT are nearly free [27]. Per-task LoRA TTT buys large reasoning gains at high per-request cost [30]. TTT layers, Titans and Hope move the loop into the architecture [28][29][52]. Test-time RL on unlabeled queries [49] sits between per-request TTT and ordinary online RL. Pick the point that matches your latency budget.
  9. Scale evaluation gates with loop speed. Cursor's frequent on-policy redeploys [34] and OpenAI's sycophancy rollback [35] show the two sides. Fast loops need automated, behavior-specific gates and a rollback path measured in minutes, not a day.

06. Human-in-the-Loop and Active Learning: Labeling Platforms, Weak Supervision, Annotation Workflows, and Expert Feedback Pipelines

Overview

Every closed-loop learning system in this atlas eventually has to answer the same question: where does the next unit of supervision come from, and who or what produces it? Chapters 02 and 03 cover two answers: fleet telemetry mined by a data engine, and pairwise preferences turned into a reward signal. This chapter covers the machinery between those two. It is about the human labor, the selection algorithms that decide what humans look at, and the platforms that carry that work at industrial scale.

Five families of design are covered:

  1. Active learning (AL). The model picks which unlabeled examples a human should label next, using uncertainty, disagreement or diversity. The classical theory dates to the 1990s and 2000s [1]. Deep variants appeared from 2017 [2][3][4][5][6], and there is a mature open-source tool layer [7][8][9][11][15].
  2. Programmatic weak supervision. Humans write labeling functions instead of labels, and a generative label model denoises them. This is the Snorkel line [16][17][18][19][20], which Google deployed as Snorkel DryBell [20][21].
  3. Labeling platforms. Products such as Scale AI, Labelbox, Label Studio, Prodigy and Argilla turn the loop into APIs for tasks, batches, callbacks, model-assisted pre-labeling, review queues and agreement metrics [11][12][13][14][15][26][27][28]. Model-in-the-loop data engines such as Segment Anything push the same idea until the model does most of the labeling [65][66].
  4. Quality control and aggregation. This covers gold questions, screening, consensus, reviewer tiers, the statistical aggregation of noisy annotators [29][30][31], model-based detection of label errors [32][33][34], and statistically valid estimation from a few human labels plus many model labels [67][68].
  5. Human feedback for LLMs. This runs from crowdworker preference collection with vendors (OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAssistant) [37][39][41][44][46][48] and public preference arenas [69] to expert and model-assisted feedback: process supervision with active selection [52][53], AI critics that help human raters [54][56], expert-written frontier evaluations [57], expert rubrics used as rewards and evaluation specifications [71][72][73][74], and adversarial human red-teaming programs [42][58].

The common thread is that human attention is the scarcest resource in the loop. Each design in this chapter is a way of spending it better. Some choose better examples (AL). Some move humans up a level of abstraction (weak supervision, guidelines, constitutions). Some build better tools (pre-labeling, critics). Some measure and correct human error (aggregation, confident learning).

A note on sourcing: this chapter relies on primary papers, official repositories, model cards and vendor SDK documentation. Numbers the sources report as approximate, or that are drawn from paper abstracts, are flagged as such.

1. Reference architecture of a human-in-the-loop (HITL) labeling loop

Published systems differ in emphasis, but most of them instantiate the same set of components:

            +-------------------------------------------------------------+
            |                  UNLABELED POOL / STREAM                    |
            |   (logs, fleet data, API prompts, model samples, documents) |
            +------------------------------+------------------------------+
                                           |
                     +---------------------v---------------------+
                     | SELECTOR: random | uncertainty | diversity |
                     | QBC | error-mining | policy samples (RLHF)  |
                     +---------------------+---------------------+
                                           |  batch of tasks
          +--------------------------------v-------------------------------+
          | ROUTER: crowd | vendor workforce | in-house experts | LLM judge |
          |  (skills, qualification, cost, confidentiality, overlap k)     |
          +-------+--------------------------------------------+-----------+
                  |                                            |
       +----------v-----------+                     +----------v-----------+
       | ANNOTATION UI        |  pre-labels from    | PROGRAMMATIC SOURCES |
       | (+ model pre-labels, |<--- current model --| labeling functions,  |
       |  interactive tools)  |                     | heuristics, KBs, LLMs|
       +----------+-----------+                     +----------+-----------+
                  |  raw labels                                | noisy votes
       +----------v--------------------------------------------v-----------+
       | QA + AGGREGATION: gold checks, agreement, review/reject,          |
       | Dawid-Skene / label model, confident-learning error flags         |
       +----------------------------------+--------------------------------+
                                          |  labels + provenance + confidence
                        +-----------------v------------------+
                        | LABEL STORE (versioned, auditable) |
                        +-----------------+------------------+
                                          |
                        +-----------------v------------------+
                        | TRAIN / EVAL -> new model version  |----> back to SELECTOR
                        +------------------------------------+       and pre-labeler

Three properties separate mature loops from ad-hoc ones:

  • Provenance per label. This means worker id, batch, guideline version, model version used for pre-labeling, and confidence. OpenAI's released summarization comparisons carry exactly these fields (worker, batch, split, a 1 to 9 confidence, and a free-text note) [38]. PRM800K labels record labeler, timestamp, generation, and whether the item was a quality-control or screening question [53].
  • Closed QA sub-loops. A rejected annotation must go somewhere. Label Studio's reviewer can reject with "No Rework", "Return to Annotator" or "Pass to Another Annotator" [14]. Scale's task API exposes an audit_task(accept|reject, comment) call [26].
  • Coupling between model and selector. The current model both pre-labels and chooses what to label next. That coupling is the source of AL's gains and of its main failure modes (Section 2.4).

2. Active learning: selecting what humans label

2.1 Problem and classical taxonomy

Labels are expensive, and most unlabeled examples are redundant. Settles' survey [1] remains the standard map of the field. It defines three scenarios:

  • Pool-based. Score a large unlabeled pool and pick the best examples. This is the common industrial case.
  • Stream-based selective sampling. Decide label or skip as each example arrives. This fits online systems and fleet triggers.
  • Membership query synthesis. The learner generates its own query points. It is rarely used with humans because synthesized inputs can be meaningless to annotators.

It also groups query strategies into these families [1]:

Strategy Score for candidate x Strengths Known weaknesses
Least confidence 1 - P(y_hat given x) Trivial to compute Ignores the rest of the distribution
Margin gap between top-2 class probabilities Good default for multiclass Still myopic, outlier-prone
Entropy H(P(y given x)) Uses full distribution Favors noisy or ambiguous items
Query-by-committee (QBC) vote entropy or KL disagreement among an ensemble Model-agnostic, captures epistemic uncertainty Cost of K models
Expected model change expected gradient length Targets impactful items Expensive; scale-sensitive
Expected error / variance reduction expected future loss on the pool Directly optimizes objective Usually intractable at scale
Density-weighted informativeness x representativeness Avoids outliers Needs good similarity metric
BALD (Bayesian) [2] mutual information between y and model params Separates epistemic from aleatoric Needs approximate posterior (MC dropout, ensembles)
Core-set [4] k-center coverage in embedding space Batch diversity, no uncertainty needed Embedding quality, high-dim distances
BADGE [5] k-means++ over gradient embeddings Mixes uncertainty and diversity Gradient embedding cost

Settles also lists the practical issues that decide whether AL works in production [1]:

  • Batch-mode querying. Real annotation is batched, so the top-k most uncertain items are often near-duplicates.
  • Noisy oracles. Annotators make mistakes, and hard items are the ones they get wrong most often.
  • Variable labeling costs. Uncertain items often take longer to label.
  • Stopping criteria. Knowing when further labeling stops paying off.

2.2 Deep active learning

Softmax confidence from deep networks is poorly calibrated, so the deep-AL literature substitutes better uncertainty estimates or diversity objectives:

  • Deep Bayesian AL (Gal, Islam, Ghahramani, 2017) [2] uses Monte Carlo dropout as an approximate posterior. It computes BALD, entropy and variation ratios from T stochastic forward passes, and showed these acquisition functions beat random selection on image tasks.
  • BatchBALD (2019) [3] scores the joint mutual information of a batch, so it avoids picking items that are each informative on their own but redundant with one another.
  • Core-set (Sener and Savarese, 2017) [4] reframes batch selection as k-center coverage in the network's embedding space. It is a diversity-first approach that does not depend on calibrated uncertainty.
  • BADGE (Ash et al., 2019) [5] embeds each candidate as the gradient of the loss with respect to the last layer under the model's predicted label. Gradient magnitude encodes uncertainty and direction encodes diversity. k-means++ seeding then picks a batch.
  • Stochastic batch acquisition (Kirsch et al., 2021) [6] shows that sampling from a softmax or power distribution over acquisition scores, instead of taking the top-k, is a cheap way to get batch diversity. In the authors' experiments it often matches more expensive joint or diversity methods such as BatchBALD and BADGE at a small fraction of their compute.
  • Baal (ElementAI, later independent) [7] packages MC dropout, MC DropConnect, deep ensembles and semi-supervised variants. Its accompanying paper is explicitly about "tips and tricks to make active learning usable in production".

2.3 Production AL loops in tools

Several tools implement the loop directly:

  • Label Studio implements the loop with an ML backend SDK exposing predict() and fit() [11][12]. In the Enterprise edition:
    • Each created or updated annotation fires a webhook that retrains the backend.
    • When the annotator moves on, Label Studio fetches fresh predictions for the next task.
    • "Uncertainty task sampling" orders the queue so annotators always see the tasks with the lowest prediction scores from the latest model version [11].
    • The open-source Community edition cannot do this live. It degrades to batched AL: fetch predictions, sort the data manager by prediction score, label for a while, retrain, and repeat [11].
    • This split is a useful reminder that AL needs orchestration infrastructure, not just a scoring function.
  • Label Studio's backend catalog distinguishes three capabilities per model [12]: pre-annotation, interactive mode (for example SAM 2 click-to-segment, Grounding DINO prompts, GLiNER), and training on submitted annotations. Interactive models move the human from drawing to correcting, which is a different lever from selection.
  • Prodigy (Explosion) builds its ner.teach and textcat.teach recipes around binary accept/reject decisions on model suggestions, with "the model in the loop" deciding what to ask next [15]. The recipe source exposes the sorter. Swapping prefer_uncertain() for prefer_high_scores() turns uncertainty sampling into high-score mining. Companion recipes (ner.correct, ner.silver-to-gold) turn binary "silver" annotations into complete "gold" ones [15].
  • modAL [8] (scikit-learn based) and small-text [9] (text classification with transformers) expose AL as composable query strategy, classifier and stopping-criterion components. small-text's v2.0 line (still an alpha development release as of v2.0.0.dev4, May 2026) adds refined interfaces, vector indices and new query strategies [9].
  • cleanlab [34] includes ActiveLab, "active learning with data re-labeling", for multi-annotator settings. It decides whether the next label should go to a new example or to re-labeling an existing one.

2.4 Failure modes and lessons

  • Cold start. Uncertainty from a model trained on a few dozen labels is mostly noise, so practitioners seed with random or diversity-based samples first.
  • Sampling bias and model coupling. The labeled set is no longer i.i.d. It is shaped by one model's blind spots. A different future architecture may benefit less from that data than from a random sample of equal size.
  • Batch redundancy. Naive top-k selection picks near-duplicates. Joint (BatchBALD), diversity (core-set, BADGE) or stochastic (power sampling) acquisition fixes this [3][4][5][6].
  • Outliers and noisy oracles. Entropy maximization surfaces garbage and genuinely ambiguous items. Those are exactly the items annotators disagree on, so the information gain on paper becomes label noise in practice.
  • Evaluation contamination. If the test set is drawn from AL-selected data, metrics are biased. Keep a random, independently labeled evaluation slice.
  • Adoption reality. A community survey published at EACL 2026, co-authored by the small-text maintainers, re-examined how AL is actually used in contemporary NLP [10]. Its existence is a sign that AL's role is being renegotiated now that LLM zero-shot labeling and synthetic data compete with it for the same budget.

The durable lesson is that AL pays off most when labels are truly expensive (experts, medical, legal), the pool is large and redundant, and the selector is coupled to a review loop that can absorb the extra ambiguity it surfaces.

3. Programmatic weak supervision: the Snorkel lineage

3.1 Problem

Hand labeling hits a wall when domain experts are scarce (clinicians, lawyers, analysts), when label definitions change often, or when privacy forbids sending data out to a crowd. The Snorkel project started at Stanford in 2015 on the bet that "it would increasingly be the training data, not the models, algorithms, or infrastructure, that decided whether a machine learning project succeeded or failed" [22].

3.2 Data programming (NeurIPS 2016)

Ratner et al. [16] proposed that users write labeling functions (LFs): small programs that vote a label or abstain, such as regexes, knowledge-base lookups, heuristics or other models. The LFs' accuracies and correlations are never observed directly. Instead, a generative label model learns them from the agreement and disagreement structure of the LF outputs alone. The resulting probabilistic labels then train a discriminative end model with a noise-aware loss. Because the end model sees features the LFs do not use, it generalizes beyond LF coverage.

3.3 Snorkel (VLDB 2018) architecture

  subject-matter expert
          |
          v  writes / edits
  +-----------------------+    apply over     +-----------------------------+
  | Labeling functions    |------------------>| Label matrix L (n x m)      |
  | (patterns, KB lookups,|   unlabeled data  | entries in {-1 abstain, 0,  |
  |  heuristics, models)  |                   |  ..., k-1}                  |
  +-----------------------+                   +--------------+--------------+
          ^                                                  |
          |  LF analysis: coverage, overlap, conflict,       v
          |  empirical accuracy on a small dev set   +----------------------+
          +------------------------------------------| Label model          |
                                                     | (learns LF accuracies|
                                                     |  w/o ground truth)   |
                                                     +----------+-----------+
                                                                | P(y given L)
                                                     +----------v-----------+
                                                     | End model (deep net),|
                                                     | noise-aware loss     |
                                                     +----------------------+

Snorkel [17] made this an end-to-end system: an LF authoring interface, a label model, and LF development analytics such as coverage, overlaps, conflicts and empirical accuracy on a small development set. As reported in its abstract, a user study found that subject-matter experts built models about 2.8x faster and improved predictive performance by about 45.5% on average compared with seven hours of hand labeling. Across applications, Snorkel models came within a few percentage points of models trained on large hand-curated training sets [17].

Later components extended the paradigm:

  • Snorkel MeTaL [18] extended the label model to multi-task weak supervision, with tasks at different granularities and a matrix-completion-style estimator. The motivating vision was "massively multitask learning" with "tens or hundreds of tasks with supervision of widely varying quality". MeTaL was merged into Snorkel v0.9 in August 2019 [18].
  • Snorkel v0.9 added two more operators besides LFs. Transformation functions do data augmentation. Slicing functions monitor and up-weight critical subsets [23].
  • FlyingSquid [19] replaced iterative SGD label-model fitting with a closed-form triplet method. It solves for LF accuracies from triplets of conditionally independent LFs, and averaging over all triplets proved more stable. This makes the label model fast enough for interactive and online use.

3.4 Snorkel DryBell at Google (SIGMOD Industry 2019)

DryBell [20][21] is the canonical industrial deployment. Google adapted Snorkel to its infrastructure and used it on content and event classification tasks. The paper's running example is classifying documents for celebrity mentions [20][23]. Key design points:

  • Organizational knowledge as LFs. LFs wrapped existing internal resources: legacy models, knowledge graphs, entity taggers, aggregate statistics and heuristics. Many of these resources were non-servable. They were too slow, too expensive, or depended on features unavailable at serving time. Weak supervision distilled non-servable signals into a servable end model that uses only production features.
  • Execution at scale. The label model was re-implemented to run over millions of examples in a distributed setting. The open-source tutorials mirror this with Dask and Spark versions of the pipeline and an NLPLabelingFunction template that caches expensive NLP preprocessing [23].
  • Reported results (abstract-level, approximate). Classifiers of quality comparable to ones trained on tens of thousands of hand-labeled examples; about a 52% average improvement from converting non-servable resources into servable models; and labeling of millions of data points in tens of minutes [20].

3.5 Ecosystem and evolution

  • Snorkel Flow. The academic team shifted to a commercial platform, Snorkel Flow, extending the ideas to data slicing, monitoring, augmentation and multi-task modeling. The open-source repository now points users there [22].
  • WRENCH [24] standardized evaluation across many weak supervision datasets and label models. Its companion survey [25] organizes the field: label models, joint label and end models, and interactive LF development.
  • Overlap with crowdsourcing. The same machinery handles crowdworkers as LFs. Snorkel's crowdsourcing tutorial treats each worker as a labeling function [23]. This makes the label model a generalization of Dawid-Skene aggregation (Section 5.2).

3.6 Failure modes and lessons

  • Correlated LFs (for example, two regexes derived from one keyword list) violate independence assumptions and double-count evidence. Structure learning or careful LF design is required.
  • Coverage gaps. Examples where all LFs abstain get no signal. End-model generalization helps, but it cannot fix a systematically uncovered region.
  • A dev set is still needed. LF iteration relies on a small hand-labeled development set. Weak supervision reduces hand labeling; it does not eliminate it.
  • The human moves up a level. The highest-leverage effect is organizational. Experts encode rules and resources once, and the system re-labels everything when definitions change. That makes labeling a versioned code artifact. This same idea reappears in LLM alignment as constitutions and rubrics (Section 7.4 and Chapter 03).

4. Labeling platforms as loop infrastructure

4.1 Scale AI: the task API and the vendor workforce

Scale AI's public Python client documents the abstractions an external labeling loop needs [26]:

  • Tasks are created per task type with a callback_url (push notification on completion) and an idempotency key unique_id. Creating a duplicate raises an error, which prevents double-paying on client retries. Status moves through pending, completed, error and canceled.
  • Batches group tasks. A batch is finalized to release it to the workforce, and progress is polled through tasks_pending and tasks_completed. Tasks can be filtered by review_status, for example Accepted.
  • Audits. audit_task(id, accept, comment) mirrors Scale's Audit UI, so the customer's own QA decision feeds back to the vendor.
  • Projects come in two documented modes, Rapid and Studio (set by rapid=true or studio=true). Assignments and labeler groups are Studio-only features, which matches Studio's role as the product for customer-managed labeling teams. Rapid projects support evaluation tasks: tasks with a known expected_response that are "used to measure workers' performance internally to ensure the quality". They also support training tasks, used "to onboard taskers onto your project" [26].

Scale's role extends upstream (curation and error mining with Nucleus, covered in Chapter 02) and into LLM post-training data. Three public records show Scale as an RLHF and evaluation vendor:

  • InstructGPT's contractors were hired "through Upwork and ScaleAI" [40].
  • NVIDIA's HelpSteer2 preference data was collected with Scale AI (Section 6.5) [46].
  • Humanity's Last Exam was a joint effort of the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI [57].

The market's strategic weight showed in June 2025, when Meta took a non-voting 49% stake in Scale (reported at about $14 billion) and CEO Alexandr Wang moved to Meta [51]. That transaction raised the obvious vendor-neutrality question for frontier labs that also bought data from Scale. This is a structural risk for any loop that depends on one external workforce.

4.2 Labelbox: catalog, model-assisted labeling and LLM feedback projects

Labelbox positions itself as a platform to "curate and annotate data, generate high-quality human feedback data for computer vision and language models, evaluate and improve model performance, and automate tasks by seamlessly combining AI and human-centric workflows" [27]. Its official SDK notebooks map the loop components one-to-one [27]:

  • Curation: data rows, metadata, custom embeddings for similarity search (Catalog).
  • Pre-labeling: "Model predictions to project" and per-modality prediction upload notebooks, plus annotation import. This is model-assisted labeling, where humans correct imported predictions instead of labeling from scratch. Meta SAM integrations cover interactive segmentation.
  • Evaluation: model experiments, model slices and custom metrics. These compare model runs against ground truth to find error clusters worth relabeling.
  • Workflow: batches, queue management, webhooks, ontologies, user management.
  • LLM feedback: dedicated project types for multimodal chat evaluation, offline multimodal chat evaluation, prompt-response creation and LLM data generation [27]. These are the human-feedback collection UIs used for SFT demonstrations and preference ranking.

4.3 Label Studio: open-source core, agreement and review

Label Studio (HumanSignal) is the most widely documented open-source platform. Beyond the AL loop in Section 2.3, its Enterprise documentation is unusually explicit about QA mechanics [13][14]:

  • Agreement is computed per control tag. A task with bounding boxes, a choice field and a rating has three agreement scores. The overall score is a weighted mean, so critical fields can dominate.
  • Agreement metrics depend on data type. Categorical tags use exact match (or numeric difference with a threshold for ratings). Spatial and structural tags use IoU for boxes and polygons, and span overlap for text.
  • Two aggregation methodologies: pairwise average across annotator pairs, and consensus.
  • Review ordering. Reviewers can order their queue by annotator (to audit individuals), by agreement (low-agreement first), or by model confidence (least confident first) [14]. This turns the review queue into a second AL loop.
  • Reject routing: No Rework, Return to Annotator, or Pass to Another Annotator [14].

4.4 Argilla, Prodigy and LLM-native tooling

  • Argilla describes itself as "a collaboration tool for AI engineers and domain experts to build high-quality datasets". It is deployable on the Hugging Face Hub [28] and is used for preference and SFT data review.
  • Prodigy keeps annotation binary and fast. Accept/reject on a model suggestion is far cheaper per decision than full manual annotation [15].
  • LLM pre-labeling with confidence routing. Refuel's Autolabel [36] labels text datasets with any LLM from a JSON config of guidelines and few-shot examples. It includes cost estimation and caching, and attaches a confidence estimate to every label. The recommended pattern is to "calibrate a confidence threshold for your labeling task, and then route less confident labels to humans" [36]. The README's toy run reports roughly $0.0027 per example. This is the 2023 to 2026 successor to classical AL: the model labels everything, and humans see only what the model is unsure about.

4.5 Model-in-the-loop data engines: Segment Anything and SAM 2

Meta's Segment Anything projects are the clearest published example of a labeling loop where the model being trained is also the annotation tool, and its share of the labeling grows stage by stage.

  • SAM (2023) [65] built SA-1B, about 11 million images and 1.1 billion masks, with a three-stage data engine (counts below are as reported in the paper and approximate):
    1. Assisted-manual. Professional annotators clicked foreground and background points in a browser tool powered by an early SAM and refined the masks. The model was retrained several times on the growing data, and the reported time per mask fell from about 34 to about 14 seconds.
    2. Semi-automatic. The model pre-filled confident masks, and annotators labeled only the objects it had missed. This is a diversity-targeted selector: human effort goes to the less prominent objects.
    3. Fully automatic. The model was prompted with a regular point grid. Masks were kept by predicted IoU and stability filters, and the released dataset is almost entirely (about 99%) model-generated. Human effort shifted to quality audits of samples.
  • SAM 2 (2024) [66] repeated the pattern for video with a "model-in-the-loop data engine, which improves model and data via user interaction" [66]. The resulting SA-V dataset has about 51K videos and 643K masklets. Of the training masklets, about 190K are manual and about 452K are automatic. The validation and test masklets are manually annotated in every frame, at 6 fps [66]. The paper reports that annotating with SAM 2 in the loop was several times faster than per-frame annotation with the original SAM (approximate).

Two design points carry over to any domain. First, the human-to-model labor ratio is a schedule, not a constant, and each stage needs a different UI and QA regime. Second, the evaluation splits stay fully human-annotated even when the training data is mostly automatic, which is the same discipline as the random evaluation slice in Section 2.4.

4.6 Platform comparison

Platform Deployment AL / selection Pre-labeling QA primitives LLM feedback UIs
Scale AI [26] Managed workforce + API Customer-driven; Nucleus mining (Ch. 02) Studio / model-assisted Evaluation (gold) tasks, training tasks, audits, review status RLHF / evaluation vendor (InstructGPT, HelpSteer2, HLE)
Labelbox [27] SaaS + SDK Catalog search, model slices, metrics Prediction import (MAL), SAM Queues, review, webhooks Chat evaluation, prompt-response, LLM data generation
