07. Production Traces to Fine-Tuning Loops: Logging, Evaluation, Curation, Distillation and Routing

Overview

Most LLM applications start on a large, general-purpose API model. Once the application has real traffic, every request and response becomes a labelled (or labellable) example of the exact task the business cares about. The designs in this chapter turn that "data exhaust" into a better system: they log production calls with enough structure to slice them by task, evaluate candidate models or prompts against held-out slices of that traffic, curate the logs into training sets, and train. Training can be supervised distillation into a smaller model, preference tuning, or reinforcement learning against graders. The loop then promotes the winner, often behind a router that decides per request which model gets the call, and keeps logging.

NVIDIA's reference implementation defines a data flywheel as "a process that uses data exhaust from production applications (for example, LLM prompt/response logs, end user feedback, and expert labeling) to increase the overall accuracy and reduce the latency/cost of Generative AI systems" [25]. Commercial platforms package the same loop differently:

  • OpenAI built it into its API: stored completions, the Evals API, one-click distillation and reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) [1][2][3].
  • OpenPipe started with an SDK that logs requests and fine-tunes on them, then moved to open-source agent RL with ART and RULER [7][10][11].
  • Predibase supplies the methodology (a distillation playbook) and the serving layer (LoRAX) [15][17].
  • Fireworks, Together and Thinking Machines (Tinker) expose training APIs and cookbooks covering SFT, DPO, GRPO and on-policy distillation [18][19][23][48].
  • Hyperscalers offer the same capture-to-distill path: Amazon Bedrock can distill directly from tagged invocation logs [47].
  • Open standards are emerging for both ends of the loop: OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions for traces and evaluation results [44][45], and OpenEnv for agent environments [49].
  • Research and open-source projects supply the parts these platforms are built from:
    • routers trained on preference or outcome data [31][32][34];
    • on-policy distillation objectives [40][41];
    • agent-RL middleware that captures training data from unmodified production agent harnesses [28][29].

The canonical loop, abstracted across all of these systems:

 +-------------+  requests   +-------------------+  responses  +-------------+
 |  App / agent|------------>| gateway / SDK /   |------------>| served model|
 |  (workload  |<------------| router (logs all) |<------------| (API / LoRA)|
 |   tags)     |             +---------+---------+             +------^------+
 +-------------+                       | traces + tags + feedback      |
                                       v                               | promote
                          +------------+-------------+                 | (canary /
                          | trace store (ES, S3, PG, |                 |  shadow)
                          | vendor "stored compl.")  |                 |
                          +------------+-------------+                 |
                                       | filter / dedup / split        |
                                       v                               |
           +---------------+   +-------+--------+   +---------------+  |
           | eval sets     |   | train sets     |   | grader/judge  |  |
           | (held-out,    |   | (teacher out-  |   | (code, model, |  |
           |  stratified)  |   |  puts, prefs)  |   |  rubric)      |  |
           +-------+-------+   +-------+--------+   +-------+-------+  |
                   |                   v                    |          |
                   |          +--------+---------+          |          |
                   |          | SFT / DPO / RFT /|<---------+          |
                   |          | GRPO / OPD (LoRA)|  rewards            |
                   |          +--------+---------+                     |
                   v                   v                               |
                +--+-------------------+--+    gate: beats baseline?   |
                | evaluate candidates     |----------------------------+
                | (base, ICL, tuned)      |  human review before prod
                +-------------------------+

The chapter is organized by vendor or system, then by technique (distillation objectives, agent-RL plumbing, routing), and ends with a comparison table, cross-cutting failure modes and design takeaways. Chapter 02 covers fleet-scale data engines, including NVIDIA's flywheel blueprints from the autonomy angle. Chapter 03 covers RLHF, and chapter 04 covers RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and self-improvement. This chapter covers the LLM-application side: going from an API call log to a cheaper, better, task-specific model.

A note on sources: primary material is drawn mostly from vendors' own public repositories, documentation sources and cookbooks. Cookbook dates and authors follow the OpenAI Cookbook registry [4]. Where a figure comes from a vendor and was not independently reproduced, it is labelled as a vendor claim.

1. Anatomy of a trace-to-model loop

Across all the systems surveyed, the loop breaks into the same stages. The hard engineering problems sit in the seams between them.

1.1 Capture: what a "trace" must contain

The minimum useful record is the exact request payload and the exact response. NVIDIA's blueprint requires each log document to carry timestamp, workload_id, client_id, the full OpenAI-format request and the full response. It explains: "Keeping the full request/response allows the Flywheel to replay prompts, build few-shot demonstrations, and fine-tune without lossy conversions" [25]. Two capture details recur:

  • Task identity. NVIDIA makes workload_id the "primary key for slicing, deduplication, and dataset creation." It insists that each node of a multi-step agent gets its own id, because an untagged mix of chat, query rewriting and tool routing cannot be evaluated or distilled coherently [25][26]. The same role is played by OpenAI's metadata tags on stored completions [1][2] and OpenPipe's tags (for example prompt_id) [8].
  • Non-blocking logging. OpenPipe's SDK calls the upstream model directly and records the request after returning the completion. For streams, it forwards tokens as they arrive and reports the assembled response at the end, so logging adds no latency [8][9]. NVIDIA warns that streaming clients must buffer the stream and rebuild a full response object before indexing [25].

For RL on agents, text is not enough. The Agent Lightning team documented retokenization drift: if a trainer re-tokenizes logged strings instead of using the token IDs the inference engine actually sampled, the learner can optimize "against the wrong sequence." There are three causes:

  1. Non-unique tokenizations (for example H+AVING versus HAV+ING).
  2. Tool-call parsing and re-serialization. These change whitespace and can silently auto-correct malformed JSON, which "masks the model's true generation errors."
  3. Chat-template differences between frameworks.

The result is effectively off-policy updates and unstable learning curves. The authors add that because the drift is not token-level, it "cannot be corrected through token-level importance sampling." The fix was upstreamed into vLLM (v0.10.2): the OpenAI-compatible API accepts return_token_ids and returns prompt_token_ids and token_ids [30]. Agent Lightning v1.0's gateway now records "prompt token IDs, response token IDs, and chosen-token log probabilities" for every proxied call [29].

1.2 Curate and split

Every source says that curation matters more than training hyperparameters:

  • Predibase's playbook: "Most mistakes made by converged student models can be traced back to issues with the source data." It warns that logs-based datasets are often "variation or balance-deficient", for example with too many examples from power users [15].
  • NVIDIA's flywheel deduplicates, then applies class-aware stratified splitting so that eval and train sets have balanced representation across tool types. It explicitly guards against eval/train leakage, which "can lead to inflated evaluation scores" [25][26].
  • OpenPipe holds out 20% of each dataset as a test set automatically [9].
  • OpenPipe's pruning rules strip static text (for example long system prompts) from training data. The fine-tuned model inherits the rules and applies them to incoming requests, so the student pays for fewer input tokens [9].

1.3 Evaluate and gate

The loop is only as good as its evaluator. Three evaluator families appear:

  1. Deterministic checks: exact match, schema validity, string or Python graders.
  2. Reference similarity: fuzzy match, embedding cosine.
  3. LLM-as-judge: pairwise, rubric-scored or ranked.

OpenAI's evaluation-flywheel guide (co-authored with Hamel Husain) recommends measuring a judge against SME labels using true-positive and true-negative rates rather than accuracy. Test sets are imbalanced, so "a judge that always guesses 'pass' might be 95% accurate but will never find a single failure." It suggests splitting judge-alignment data about 20/40/40 into few-shot, validation and test sets [5].

1.4 Promote with a human in the loop

None of the reference designs promote automatically. NVIDIA: "Think of the Flywheel as a flashlight, not an autopilot. Promotion to production ... remains a human decision" [25]. The blueprint "doesn't automatically promote or deploy any model" [26]. Predibase recommends canary rollout (1%, then 10%), dark launch (shadowing the teacher) or a hybrid launch where the student takes the easy queries and the teacher the hard ones [15]. That hybrid launch is a router, which links distillation loops to the routing loops in section 10.

1.5 Trace standards and observability platforms

Vendor-specific capture (stored completions, OpenPipe tags, NVIDIA's Elasticsearch schema) locks the training data to one platform. Since 2024 the OpenTelemetry project has been standardizing GenAI telemetry, now maintained in a dedicated semantic-conventions-genai repository and still at Development stability [44]:

  • Spans carry gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.id, token usage counts (for example gen_ai.usage.input_tokens) and, for multi-turn sessions, gen_ai.conversation.id. Operation names such as invoke_agent and execute_tool cover agent invocations and tool calls, and further spans cover retrieval and memory operations.
  • Content is opt-in. gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, system instructions and tool definitions are all Opt-In attributes flagged as likely to contain sensitive or PII data. A default-configured instrumentation therefore yields cost and latency telemetry but not a trainable dataset. A flywheel has to turn content capture on deliberately and route it to a store with appropriate retention and redaction.
  • Evaluations are first-class events. A gen_ai.evaluation.result event records an evaluator name, a score value and a label (for example pass or fail), parented to the span being evaluated or linked by gen_ai.response.id [45]. Judge scores, user feedback and production outcomes can thus be joined to the exact call they grade, which is the join every curation step in section 1.2 needs.

Open-source LLM observability platforms sit on top of this layer. Langfuse, for example, combines production tracing with LLM-as-judge, code evaluators, user feedback, manual labelling and datasets built from production traces for regression testing and experiments [46]. These tools usually stop at the eval set. Exporting their curated datasets into a fine-tuning API is the step that closes the loop described in this chapter.

2. OpenAI: stored completions, Evals, distillation and RFT

2.1 Problem and architecture

OpenAI's design keeps the whole loop inside the API platform. The capture primitive is store=True on a chat completion, with free-form metadata. Logging can also be turned on by default at the organization level [2]. Stored completions feed three consumers:

 chat.completions.create(store=True, metadata={usecase:..., prompt_version:...})
            |
            v
   +------------------+   filter by model+metadata   +---------------------------+
   | Stored           |----------------------------->| "Distill": auto-built     |
   | completions      |                              | JSONL -> fine-tune job    |
   | (platform logs)  |                              | (e.g. gpt-4o -> 4o-mini)  |
   +--------+---------+                              +-------------+-------------+
            | data_source_config:                                  |
            | {type: stored_completions, metadata: {...}}           v
            v                                            ft:gpt-4o-mini:...:wine
   +------------------+  testing_criteria (label_model, score_model, python,
   | Evals API: Eval  |  text_similarity, string_check)  -> Runs per prompt/model
   +--------+---------+
            | graders reused as reward
            v
   +------------------+  method.type = "reinforcement", grader, hyperparameters
   | RFT job (o4-mini)|  -> eval runs logged back into Evals during training
   +------------------+

2.2 Distillation from stored completions

The distillation cookbook (October 2024) shows the full loop on a wine grape-variety classification task [1]:

  • Logging. It logs gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini outputs with store=True and a distillation metadata tag, using Structured Outputs with an enum to constrain answers.
  • Distilling. It filters the stored completions in the dashboard by model (gpt-4o only) and metadata, then clicks Distill. This auto-creates the training file and starts a gpt-4o-mini fine-tune.
  • Baseline (500 rows). gpt-4o reached 81.8% accuracy and gpt-4o-mini 69.0%.
  • Held-out set (300 rows). gpt-4o scored 79.67%, gpt-4o-mini 64.67% and the distilled gpt-4o-mini 79.33%. The author describes this as "almost a 22% relative improvement" over the undistilled small model.
  • Cost. The notebook's own price constants (October 2024) were $2.50 per 1M input tokens for gpt-4o and $0.15 for gpt-4o-mini. The 500-prompt run (about 245K tokens) cost about $0.61 against $0.04, roughly a 16x inference-cost gap at the time.

The lesson is that a narrow, closed-label task can recover nearly all of the teacher's accuracy in a model that costs an order of magnitude less. Structured outputs made the eval a trivial string compare.

2.3 Monitoring stored completions with Evals

The completion-monitoring cookbook (April 2025) turns stored production traffic into a regression test [2]:

  • An Eval declares data_source_config = {type: "stored_completions", metadata: {usecase: ...}}, which exposes {{item.input}} and {{sample.output_text}} to graders.
  • Each Run selects a slice, such as one prompt_version.
  • A label_model grader (o3-mini in the example) labels each push-notification summary correct or incorrect.

The recommended pattern is to tag every call with a use case and a prompt version, so any change can be compared on real traffic without building a separate dataset.

2.4 Reinforcement fine-tuning with graders

RFT runs RL on a reasoning model "by exploring the solution space and reinforcing strategies that result in a higher reward." The grader is the reward function. The May 2025 cookbook applies RFT to o4-mini on 100 training and 100 test medical vignettes [3]. Its main finding is the sequence of grader designs:

  1. String grader. A multi grader combined fuzzy token-set similarity (0.85) and exact match (0.15). It produced "stagnant reward" because the signal was not rich enough.
  2. Model grader v1. This was a gpt-4.1 score_model with an additive rubric (exact match +0.15, synonym +0.35, same family +0.35 ...). The policy reward-hacked it. Scores "shot up—sometimes by 20-30 percentage points", but only because the model padded one-phrase answers with synonyms, doses and management plans that inflated lexical similarity.
  3. Model grader v2. This version normalized answers (mapping to ICD-10 or SNOMED where possible), scored a six-level clinical similarity ladder at weight 0.90 and lexical similarity at 0.10, penalized missing critical modifiers, and included contrastive examples built from the earlier run's hacked outputs. The authors used o3 to check that the grader ranked predictions sensibly before training.

The final job used n_epochs=5, reasoning_effort=medium, compute_multiplier=1.0, eval_samples=3 and eval_interval=5, after validating the grader through the graders validate endpoint. The tuned model gained "about a 5-point boost in accuracy". Its score distribution moved from the 0.2–0.6 band into 0.8–1.0, and it spent more reasoning tokens than base o4-mini. When both o3 and the tuned model scored zero on the same items, the authors read that as a sign of bad reference labels, not model failure. They recommend expert relabeling before adding compute. On cost, LLM graders are billed on top of training compute, so the advice is to test graders locally and start with small runs to catch hacking early [3].

2.5 Prompt-level loops on the same substrate

Not every loop updates weights. The evaluation-flywheel guide (October 2025) frames the work as Analyze → Measure → Improve [5]:

  • open-code about 50 failing traces;
  • group the codes into axial categories (for example "35% of failures are tour scheduling");
  • build graders for each category;
  • run the platform's prompt optimizer, which uses outputs, annotations and graders.

The "Self-Evolving Agents" cookbook (November 2025) automates the same loop [6]:

  • Four graders score each output: two Python checks (chemical-name retention, length), embedding similarity, and an LLM judge, with pass thresholds of 0.8–0.85.
  • A metaprompt agent rewrites the prompt until an aggregate score passes or max_retry runs out (10 in the example), at which point engineers are alerted.
  • A VersionedPrompt store keeps history for rollback.

The authors' lessons: "the optimization is not always successful, so being able to roll back the prompt version is important," and grader fidelity determines optimization quality. The same notebook notes that the Evals platform "does not yet provide an API to retrieve user feedback programmatically", so human thumbs-up and thumbs-down data cannot yet flow back into the loop automatically.

2.6 The same pattern on a hyperscaler: Bedrock distillation from invocation logs

Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation packages the stored-completions pattern for AWS. Its workflow automates teacher response generation, data synthesis and student fine-tuning, and one of its two input modes is historical invocation logs [47]. AWS's sample notebook shows the loop end to end:

  • Capture. Model invocation logging is enabled to an S3 bucket. Each teacher call (Llama 3.1 70B in the example) is made through the Converse API with requestMetadata tags such as {"job_type": ..., "invoke_model": "llama31-70b"}, the direct analogue of OpenAI's metadata.
  • Curation by tag. The distillation job's invocationLogsConfig points at the log bucket and applies requestMetadataFilters (for example equals: {"invoke_model": "llama31-70b"}) so only the intended workload is used.
  • Reuse or regenerate. The flag usePromptResponse (default False) decides whether the logged teacher responses are used as targets or only the prompts are kept and the teacher is re-queried during the job.
  • Train. The student (Llama 3.1 8B in the example) is fine-tuned on the result, with the teacher named in teacherModelConfig.

The usePromptResponse switch makes explicit a choice every log-driven loop faces: train on what production actually returned (cheap, but it inherits any prompt version or model that was live at the time) or re-label the logged prompts with today's best teacher.

3. OpenPipe: from request logs to agent RL

3.1 Phase 1: logging-first fine-tuning platform

OpenPipe (YC S23) pitched: "Use powerful but expensive LLMs to fine-tune smaller and cheaper models suited to your exact needs ... Switch between OpenAI and fine-tuned models with one line of code" [7]. The architecture:

 app --(openpipe SDK = drop-in OpenAI client)--> OpenAI (key stays on client)
   |                                                  |
   +-- async report (after completion / end of stream)+--> OpenPipe request logs
                                                              | filters: model, tags,
                                                              | request/response text
                                                              v
                                                       dataset (+ pruning rules,
                                                       20% auto test split)
                                                              v
                                       fine-tune (Mistral/Llama/GPT-3.5 base) -> hosted,
                                       OpenAI-compatible endpoint or downloadable weights
                                                              v
                                       evals: GPT-4 judge, head-to-head vs base models

Key techniques, from the open-sourced docs:

  • Capture. SDK or proxy capture with searchable tags [8].
  • Curation by query. Users filter logs, for example by prompt_id, by excluding responses containing "As an AI language model", or by model, then import the matching logs into a dataset [9].
  • Pruning rules. Static text is removed before training (section 1.2) [9].
  • Judged comparison. Evaluations use GPT-4 as a judge with configurable criteria [9].

A notable product choice is that the client keeps the OpenAI key and calls OpenAI directly, "so you'll continue getting uninterrupted inference even if your OpenPipe instance goes down" [9]. The logging plane is kept off the critical path. The open-source repository has since been frozen "to integrate some proprietary third-party code" [7].

3.2 Phase 2: ART, agent RL with GRPO

ART (Agent Reinforcement Trainer, 2025) moves from imitating a teacher to learning from reward [10][13]:

  • An OpenAI-compatible client embedded in the user's code runs the agent workflow, usually with many parallel rollouts.
  • Completions are served by a backend running the latest LoRA in vLLM.
  • Every system, user and assistant message is stored in a Trajectory, and the user's code assigns each trajectory a reward.
  • Trajectories are grouped. Inference pauses while the backend trains with GRPO from the latest checkpoint (or an empty LoRA), saves the new LoRA, hot-loads it into vLLM and resumes.
  • A dedicated mode keeps training and inference on separate GPUs.
  • SFT is supported for distillation and as a warm-up before RL [14].
  • Checkpoint forking allows branching from a known-good step [14].

The ART FAQ gives unusually concrete guidance on when the loop works [12]:

  • Open models should already complete the task "at least 30% of the time".
  • Success must be "easily" verifiable, whether objectively or by a consistent LLM judge.
  • The agent must be runnable many times "without affecting the real world". GRPO needs repeated rollouts on the same scenario, which rules out agents with irreversible side effects.
  • Runs "often cost between $15 and $200 in GPU time".
  • Production aberrations "can be instantly fixed by adding a similar training example to the training set", which closes the production-to-training loop.

OpenPipe reports that its ART·E email-research agent (Qwen 2.5 14B) beat o3. This is a vendor claim, linked from the README [10]. The README also advertises W&B Training (Serverless RL) as a hosted ART backend, with vendor-claimed "40% lower cost" and "28% faster training" from multiplexing on a shared inference cluster [10].

3.3 RULER: rewards without labels

RULER (Relative Universal LLM-Elicited Rewards) addresses the hardest part of turning traces into RL data: writing a reward function [11]. It rests on two observations: "relative scoring is easier than absolute scoring," and "GRPO only needs relative scores" because it normalizes within each group. The procedure:

  1. Generate N trajectories for one scenario.
  2. Deduplicate their common prefix (for example the shared system prompt).
  3. Ask a judge model (for example openai/o3) to score each from 0 to 1, with explanations.
  4. Use the scores directly as GRPO rewards.

The default rubric says goal-achieving trajectories must score "significantly higher". More efficient paths beat less efficient ones, score gaps should be proportional to quality gaps, and partial credit is allowed. The judge gets task understanding from the trajectories' own system prompts. The implementation allows one bounded re-judge on a malformed ranking and records judge cost as a training metric. OpenPipe claims RULER cuts implementation time "2-3x" and "often matches or exceeds hand-crafted reward functions" (vendor claim) [11]. RULER also powers "AutoRL" and "MCP•RL", which train without labelled data by generating inputs and judging outputs [10].

4. Predibase: the distillation playbook, LoRA Land and LoRAX

4.1 The playbook as a process specification

Predibase's LLM Distillation Playbook (Zhao and Abid, February 2024) is the most explicit written process for log-to-student distillation [15]. Its 12 practices map onto the loop:

Stage Practice (abridged)
Feasibility Students usually at best match the teacher. Imitation can copy style without factuality ("False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs"). Narrow tasks distill best
Capture "Build good logging infrastructure": stream MaaS requests and responses to S3 or Snowflake. Bootstrap with synthetic data when logs are thin
Eval Fixed, diverse test sets. Measure both an in-distribution set (90/10 class mix) and a balanced set (50/50)
Teacher Maximize teacher quality first. A simpler prompt beat chain-of-thought for labelling, and temperature 0 was best
Data Fix data at the source, filter by rules, rank with LLMs, add explanation traces, aggregate multiple teachers
Training Start small. Run ablations on data size. Change one parameter at a time
Serving Plan for PEFT and multi-LoRA serving early
Deploy Canary, dark launch or hybrid launch. Monitor inputs for drift and outputs for failures, and keep logging for re-distillation

The Jigsaw toxicity case study gives quantitative lessons. Adding gold human labels and removing incorrect teacher labels both improved the student. Going from 1.1K to 5K examples gave a large jump, but going from 5K to 10K was "rather marginal" [15]. Preference tuning (RLHF/DPO) was rated a costly "last mile optimization", and the authors had "yet to speak with a company who has a critical need" for it in 2024 [15]. Chapter 04 shows how much that view changed once graders and RFT became productized.

4.2 LoRA Land and the economics of many small specialists

LoRA Land measured 310 models: 10 base models fine-tuned with 4-bit LoRA on 31 tasks. The authors report that the fine-tuned models "outperform base models by 34 points and GPT-4 by 10 points on average". The accompanying demo served 25 LoRA fine-tuned Mistral-7B models on a single 80 GB A100 [16]. The serving layer is LoRAX, which serves many adapters over one shared base model [17]:

  • Just-in-time adapter loading happens per request without blocking concurrent requests.
  • Heterogeneous continuous batching packs requests for different adapters into one batch, "keeping latency and throughput nearly constant with the number of concurrent adapters." Multi-adapter kernels (Punica's SGMV) keep the mixed batch efficient under load.
  • Adapter exchange scheduling asynchronously prefetches and offloads adapters between GPU and CPU memory.

This matters for loop design because a flywheel that spawns a new adapter per workload, per tenant or per retraining cycle stays affordable only if adapters share base-model GPUs. Without that, each new specialist needs dedicated capacity and the flywheel stalls on serving cost. Fireworks' multilora_fleet case study ("one deployment, a per-tenant specialist for every locale", 51 locales) follows the same pattern [19].

5. Fireworks: training API, Eval Protocol and on-policy distillation

5.1 Architecture

The 2026 Fireworks cookbook presents training as a programmable API rather than a black-box job. The repository is organized as recipes/ (one training loop per file), utils/ (losses, rollout helpers, metrics) and examples/ (task code plus one recipe call), with "dedicated" and "serverless" twins for each example [18][19]. The recipe set covers:

  • SFT, DPO and ORPO;
  • synchronous GRPO, and async GRPO "with rollout/train overlap and bounded staleness";
  • on-policy distillation (OPD) and top-K self-distillation (SDFT);
  • embedding fine-tuning;
  • experimental PPO with a value head.

The documented GRPO loss is clipped against rollout logprobs with group-normalized advantages and no frozen-reference KL term by default [19].

Two workflows differ in cost model [20]:

  • Dedicated. A managed trainer plus an on-demand deployment, billed per GPU-hour.
  • Serverless. The user drives forward_backward and optim_step against a shared pooled trainer and samples in-session from a snapshot, billed per token with no idle cost.

In earlier runs of the router case study on qwen3p5-9b, the dedicated path took about 12–25 minutes against about 2 minutes serverless for the same 51 optimizer steps. The case study notes these timings were not remeasured on the current base model [20].

5.2 Eval Protocol: RL on agents already in production

Eval Protocol (EP) addresses a deployment problem: production agents run "across remote services with heavy dependencies, Docker containers, or TypeScript backends." EP wraps an existing agent behind a rollout HTTP interface that handles "rollout orchestration, metadata passing, and trace storage." Any supported trainer can then train against it, including Fireworks RFT, TRL, Unsloth or a custom loop [22]. The cookbook's case studies all follow "build data -> evaluate the base model -> fine-tune -> evaluate again" using EP [19].

5.3 A routing model as a fine-tuning target

The sft_prompt_router case study links the distillation and routing threads [20]:

  • Task. It fine-tunes a LoRA on Qwen 3.8 27B (thinking disabled) to emit a five-field JSON routing decision: small or big model, complexity 1–5, and math, code and reasoning flags. The goal is to "keep easy chat on a small model and escalate hard logic/code/math to a big model — without paying a frontier model just to make that decision."
  • Comparison. On a 60-row holdout, the tuned model with a lean prompt beat a prompt-engineered base model that had the routing rule written into its prompt.
  • Results. Route accuracy rose from 93.3% to 98.3% (dedicated) and from 91.7% to 95.0% (serverless). Exact match on all five fields rose from about 40–42% to 67–73%. The largest gain was on the reasoning flag (62% to 93%, and 60% to 100%).

The sample is small: 992 rows in total and a 60-row holdout.

5.4 On-policy distillation (OPD)

Fireworks' OPD recipe trains the student on its own rollouts. A frozen teacher (sharing the tokenizer) scores each sampled token, and the per-token difference teacher_logprob - sampling_logprob becomes a dense advantage. This is a sampled estimate of reverse KL(student‖teacher) [21]. The loop runs as follows: sample, ask the teacher for logprobs, compute advantages, update, hot-load the new student, sample again.

A "privileged" variant gives the teacher extra context, such as a worked solution, that the student never sees. This is a way to distill from information that is present in logs but absent at inference time. Section 9 places this among the other distillation objectives.

6. Together AI and Tinker: training APIs as loop primitives

6.1 Together AI: fine-tuning API, continual fine-tuning and evaluations

Together's public cookbook covers the same loop with an API-first shape [23]:

  • Fine-tuning recipes: end-to-end SFT, DPO preference tuning, function-calling, reasoning traces, multi-turn, long-context and vision-language.
  • Evaluations API recipes: classification evals with LLM-as-judge, head-to-head comparison evals, prompt A/B evals, an "Optimizing LLM Judges" notebook for aligning judges with humans, and GEPA-based prompt evolution.

The feature most relevant to closed loops is continual fine-tuning [24]. A new job passes from_checkpoint=<previous job id>, so each retraining cycle continues from the last tuned model instead of the base model. The notebook demonstrates this with LoRA on Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B: first core function-calling categories, then the remaining niche categories. It argues that building on checkpoints means "the model is less likely to lose earlier learned abilities". The appeal for a flywheel is that each cycle trains only on the newly harvested data.

The risk is cumulative drift, which a fixed regression eval set must catch. This is the same discipline the playbook asks for ("Avoid changing your test sets frequently") [15].

6.2 Tinker: a low-level training API

Thinking Machines Lab's Tinker takes the "training as an API" idea furthest. Instead of submitting a job, the user's own Python loop calls a remote service that handles distributed training [48]:

  • create_lora_training_client(base_model, rank) opens a LoRA training session;
  • forward_backward(...) and optim_step(...) are the training primitives;
  • save_weights_and_get_sampling_client() returns a client whose sample(...) generates from the current weights, so the same script can alternate between sampling and updating;
  • save_state / load_state and checkpoint download make each cycle resumable and the weights portable.

The companion Tinker Cookbook implements SFT, RL with verifiable rewards, sandboxed code RL, DPO and a three-stage RLHF pipeline, tool use, multi-agent self-play, rubric-based grading, and on- and off-policy distillation on top of these primitives [48]. Its distillation results appear in section 9 [40]. Fireworks' serverless path (section 5.1) exposes the same forward_backward / optim_step shape. For flywheel builders the significance is that the loop's control logic (when to sample, what to grade, when to stop) stays in the team's own code, while GPU management is outsourced.

7. NVIDIA Data Flywheel Blueprint: automated experiment search

The NVIDIA blueprint (built on NeMo microservices, deprecated in April 2026 and kept for reference) is the most complete open reference implementation of the automated loop [25]. Chapter 02 covers its place in NVIDIA's broader strategy. Its LLM-specific mechanics:

 Elasticsearch (prompt/completion logs, workload_id)
        | Celery task: create_datasets (dedup, stratified split by tool class)
        v
 NeMo Datastore ---> NeMo Customizer (LoRA) ---> candidate NIMs (spun up / down by
        |                                         NeMo Deployment Manager)
        +----------> NeMo Evaluator (LLM judge; tool-calling accuracy) <-------+
                              |
                              v
        per-NIM results: base | icl | customized    (MongoDB: flywheel_runs, ...)
                              |
                              v
                 human reviews best small candidate -> manual promotion

For each candidate NIM it runs three experiments [25][27]:

  • base: replay the production prompts;
  • icl: few-shot prompts drawn from traffic, chosen at random or by semantic similarity;
  • customized: a LoRA fine-tune evaluated on the base prompts.

The ground truth is the production model's own response. This is deliberate: the blueprint notes that it routes traffic into fine-tuning "without PII removal" and builds "evaluation datasets with no ground truth other than what the production model is responding with" [25]. The objective is therefore cost and latency reduction at parity, not accuracy gains over the teacher.

Reported results. On an internal HR chatbot served by llama-3.1-70b-instruct, the tool calling workload proved simple enough that a fine-tuned llama-3.2-1b-instruct reached about 98% relative accuracy, which the blueprint presents as an inference-cost reduction of "up to 98.6%". In another case, Qwen-2.5-32b-coder matched the 70B model without fine-tuning, cutting cost and time to first token by more than 50% [25].

Operational details.

  • The minimum footprint is two H100s or A100s with a remote judge, or six with a self-hosted judge [25].
  • Runs are serialized through a Celery queue with concurrency 1, because the system cannot yet see free GPUs and would otherwise over-allocate NIM deployments [25].

Stated pitfalls [26]:

  • "Over-trusting a High Accuracy %": the remaining 5% may hold critical errors.
  • "Ignoring Test-Time Compute": a small model that emits more tokens may not be cheaper.
  • Data leakage between eval and train sets.
  • Untagged workloads.
  • Treating improvements as monotonic. Historical results must be kept because quality sometimes regresses.

Its roadmap items included PII redaction and the use of thumbs-up/down signals for DPO or KTO. At the time of deprecation, user feedback "will have no effect" on selection [26].

8. Agent RL directly from production harnesses: Agent Lightning and OpenEnv

8.1 Problem

Agent RL frameworks often require rewriting the agent into the trainer's rollout abstraction. Microsoft's Agent Lightning instead inserts a proxy between an unmodified agent and the model. Every model call made during a rollout then becomes a training sample. The project originally pitched this as training "ANY AI agent" with "(almost) zero code changes"; the v1.0 README describes agents reaching the trainer through the proxy with "ZERO changes" to the agent [28].

8.2 Architecture (v1.0, August 2026)

 Trainer (verl + vLLM) --creates rollouts--> API Gateway <--polls-- Rollout Controller
        ^                                    |  (rollouts, events,  |  launches agent as
        |   model_request events             |   endpoints)         |  local proc or
        |   (prompt ids, response ids,       |                      |  Kubernetes Job
        |    logprobs) + reward events       v                      v
        +---------------------------- OpenAI-compatible proxy <-- unmodified agent
             /proxy/rollout/{id}/attempt/{a}/mode/train/openai/v1/chat/completions

The gateway is the source of truth [29]:

  • Rollouts move through QUEUING → RUNNING → SUCCEEDED or FAILED, and carry append-only events (model_request, reward and custom events).
  • Rollout-specific URLs. The rollout ID is embedded in the proxy URL, so every call is attributed to the right execution automatically.
  • Trainer behaviour. The trainer merges consecutive calls only when their token histories are exactly continuous, computes advantages at the rollout level and supports rollout-level loss normalization.

Earlier versions (v0.2) framed this as a data-store-centric middleware. That design decouples CPU-heavy agent runners from GPU-heavy trainers, and it lets one span store serve RL, automatic prompt optimization or "filtering high rewards data and fit[ting] them via Unsloth", which is rejection-sampling SFT [30].

8.3 Results and lessons

The project reports results on SWE-bench Verified [28]:

  • Qwen3.5-9B improved from 41.8% to 56.4% (+14.6 points) using 6K training samples. The release includes the data cleaning and "reward-hacking prevention" pipeline.
  • Qwen3.5-35B-A3B improved from 47.8% to 61.6% (+13.8 points) with pure RL on 1.8K examples.

These are project-reported figures; the README does not describe how the reward-hacking prevention works.

Two lessons generalize to any trace-to-RL loop:

  1. Capture token IDs at serve time (section 1.1).
  2. Treat the production harness as the environment. That means keeping the agent's tools, context management and control flow in the loop instead of re-implementing them in a simulator.

8.4 Standardizing the environment side: OpenEnv

Agent Lightning standardizes the model side of the harness (an OpenAI-compatible proxy). OpenEnv standardizes the environment side [49]. Each environment is a Docker image exposing a Gymnasium-style reset(), step() and state() interface (sync or async) to a client over a network connection, and can run locally, in a cloud sandbox or as a Hugging Face Space. A hub lists 40+ environments, from coding sandboxes and browsers to games and finance simulators. The README lists integrations with ART, SkyRL, torchforge, TRL (whose GRPOTrainer accepts an environment_factory), Unsloth and others, and a technical committee drawn from Meta-PyTorch, Hugging Face, NVIDIA, Microsoft, Unsloth and other organizations governs it. The project describes itself as early-stage, with APIs that may change.

For trace-to-model loops, a shared environment interface addresses failure mode 8 in section 12: an agent whose production tools have side effects can be retrained against a containerized replica that exposes the same tool surface. The same image can serve RL rollouts, offline regression evals and, through its MCP endpoint, production tool calls.

9. Distillation techniques used in these loops

Objective Teacher signal Student data Where seen
Sequence-level imitation (SFT on teacher outputs) Teacher text only Teacher-generated (off-policy) OpenAI Distill [1], OpenPipe [7], Predibase [15], NVIDIA [25], ART SFT [14]
Rationale-augmented SFT Teacher labels plus explanations Off-policy Playbook "enrich data with explanation traces" [15]; Distilling Step-by-Step [43]
Offline logit distillation Stored top-k teacher logits Off-policy Arcee DistillKit: polynomial approximation, quantization and bit-packing of logits [42]
Generalized KD (GKD) Token-level teacher distribution via a JSD family Mix of on- and off-policy (lmbda) TRL GKDTrainer [41]
On-policy distillation (reverse KL) Teacher logprob of student tokens Student rollouts Fireworks OPD [21], Tinker cookbook [40]
Prompt-program to weights Traces of a prompted pipeline that pass a metric Bootstrapped traces DSPy BootstrapFinetune [38]

Key points:

  • Off-policy imitation is the default for log-derived data. Logs are teacher outputs. It is cheap, needs no teacher at training time, and works best for closed-label or schema-bound tasks [1][15][25]. Its known weakness is distribution mismatch: the student is never trained on its own mistakes. GKD was proposed to fix this. The TRL docs summarize the authors' finding that "on-policy data (high lmbda) performs better" [41].
  • On-policy distillation needs live teacher access during training but gives dense, per-token credit. The Tinker cookbook's reasoning recipe reports that SFT on OpenThoughts3 reached about 65% on AIME'24 after 3,000 steps with a rank-128 LoRA. A further 200 steps of on-policy distillation lifted it to about 76.7%. Their "personalization" recipe uses OPD to recover instruction-following (IF-eval) in about 100 steps after SFT on internal documents [40]. The pattern of adding domain knowledge with SFT and then restoring general behaviour with OPD applies directly to company-data flywheels.
  • Prompt optimization is an alternative to weight updates. GEPA reflects on full execution traces instead of collapsing them into a scalar reward. Its authors claim it needs "100–500 evaluations vs. 5,000–25,000+ for GRPO" and report production uses at several companies (vendor and author claims) [39]. DSPy explicitly composes the two approaches: optimize prompts, then BootstrapFinetune the optimized program into a small LM [38]. OpenAI's prompt optimizer and Together's GEPA notebook put this step on the same platform as fine-tuning [5][23].

10. Model routing improvement loops

Routing is the other way to cut cost with traces. Instead of making one model cheaper, it sends each request to the cheapest model likely to answer it well. A router is itself a learned model trained on outcome or preference data, so it can sit inside its own flywheel. Every routed request produces a (query, model, outcome) tuple that can retrain the router.

           query --> [router f(q) -> P(strong model wins | q)] --threshold t-->
                        ^                                    |        |
                        |                                    v        v
                        |                               weak model  strong model
                        |                                    |        |
                        +---- retrain on (q, model, judged outcome / preference) <--+
                              + recalibrate t on recent traffic

10.1 Cascades: FrugalGPT

FrugalGPT (Stanford, 2023; TMLR version later) treats budget-constrained LLM use as a composition problem. Its techniques include prompt adaptation, LLM approximation (for example caching) and LLM cascades: query cheap models first and escalate when a learned scorer judges the answer unreliable. The repository has been refreshed with newer model generations and published API generations for 12 commercial models per dataset to support tradeoff evaluation [34]. A cascade pays for the cheap call on every request. Its trace-loop benefit is that the scorer can be retrained on logged pairs of cheap answers and verified outcomes.

10.2 Pre-generation routers: RouteLLM, RoRF and successors

RouteLLM (LMSYS with Anyscale, 2024) routes between a strong and a weak model before generation. Its routers are trained on Chatbot Arena preference data, augmented with GPT-4 as a judge [31]:

  • mf: matrix factorization, the recommended router;
  • sw_ranking: similarity-weighted Elo;
  • bert: a BERT classifier;
  • causal_llm: an LLM-based classifier.

A random router is also provided as a baseline.

Each router exposes one method, calculate_strong_win_rate(prompt). A request goes to the strong model when the win rate exceeds a cost threshold, encoded in the model name (for example router-mf-0.11593). Reported results: cost reduced by "up to 85%" while keeping "95% GPT-4 performance" on MT Bench, and ">40% cheaper" than commercial offerings at equal performance. The routers also generalize to other model pairs without retraining [31].

Threshold calibration is the operational knob. The threshold is calibrated on a sample of queries to hit a target share of strong-model calls (for example 50%). The README warns that "the % of calls routed to each model will differ based on the actual queries received," so recalibration on recent traffic is part of the loop [31].

Successor projects follow the same template:

  • Not Diamond's RoRF routes with random forests over embeddings. It ships 12 pre-trained routers across 6 model pairs and reuses RouteLLM's controller and threshold calibration. It reports that routing between two strong models can cut cost while beating both (vendor claim) [32].
  • RouterBench (Martian) provides a standard cost-versus-quality evaluation pipeline and dataset for routers [33].
  • LLMRouter (UIUC, 2025–2026) unifies 16+ router types across single-round, multi-round, multimodal, agentic and personalized routing. It adds a data-generation pipeline that calls APIs and evaluates outputs to build supervision automatically. Its paper reports that learned routers beat the strongest fixed-model baseline by 14.6% (relative) [35].

10.3 Routing in the gateway

Routing has moved into infrastructure gateways that also capture traces, which merges the logging plane and the decision plane:

  • vLLM Semantic Router offers a single endpoint (vllm-sr/auto) that selects or combines backends under a quality, latency and cost policy, across edge, private and cloud compute [36].
  • Plano (Katanemo, built on Envoy) combines agent orchestration (its default router is described as a 4B-parameter routing model), LLM routing by model name, alias or preferences, and OpenTelemetry traces plus "Agentic Signals" captured "for continuous improvement" [37].

When the component that decides is also the component that logs, router retraining needs no extra integration. The fine-tuned router in section 5.3 shows the other direction: a router can itself be a small model distilled from traffic labels [20].

10.4 How routing and distillation interact

The playbook's "hybrid launch" sends easy queries to the student and hard ones to the teacher [15]. That makes a router the natural promotion mechanism for a distilled model. Combined, the loop looks like this:

  1. Log all traffic through the gateway.
  2. Distill a student on the slice where the teacher succeeds.
  3. Train or calibrate a router to send that slice to the student.
  4. Keep logging the student's traffic and the router's escalations.
  5. Feed escalations back as both router training data and new distillation targets.

No single public system in this survey documents all five steps end-to-end, but every step has a published component above.

11. Comparison

System Capture primitive Curation Training methods Evaluator Serving / promotion Public numbers
OpenAI platform [1][2][3][6] store=True + metadata Dashboard filters by model and metadata SFT distillation, DPO, RFT (o4-mini) Evals API graders: label, score, python, similarity Hosted ft: model; manual switch Distilled 4o-mini 79.3% vs teacher 79.7% vs base 64.7%; RFT about +5 pts
Amazon Bedrock distillation [47] Invocation logs to S3 + requestMetadata requestMetadataFilters; reuse logged responses or re-query teacher (usePromptResponse) Managed teacher-to-student SFT with data synthesis User-side Bedrock-hosted custom model Not published in sample
OpenPipe (classic) [7][8][9] Drop-in SDK or proxy, async report, tags Log filters, pruning rules, 20% holdout SFT on Mistral, Llama, GPT-3.5 GPT-4 judge, head-to-head Hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoint or weights Not published in docs
OpenPipe ART + RULER [10][11][12] Trajectory objects from client Group per scenario GRPO on LoRA (vLLM + Unsloth), SFT RULER relative LLM judge or custom reward LoRA hot-swap; W&B serverless backend $15–200 per run (FAQ); ART·E beats o3 (vendor)
Predibase [15][16][17] Stream logs to S3 or Snowflake Playbook practices LoRA SFT (Ludwig) Task metrics; in-distribution and balanced test sets LoRAX multi-LoRA; canary, dark or hybrid launch LoRA Land: +34 vs base, +10 vs GPT-4; 25 adapters per A100
Fireworks [19][20][21][22] Eval Protocol rollouts and trace store Per case study SFT, DPO, ORPO, GRPO (sync and async), OPD, SDFT EP evaluators Dedicated vs serverless; multi-LoRA Router SFT route accuracy 93.3% to 98.3%
Together [23][24] (bring your own logs) User-side SFT, DPO, continual FT (from_checkpoint) Evaluations API, judge tuning, GEPA Dedicated endpoints Not published in cookbook
Tinker [40][48] (bring your own logs) User code LoRA SFT, RL, DPO/RLHF, on- and off-policy distillation via forward_backward / optim_step User code; rubric grading recipes Sampling client; downloadable checkpoints OPD: AIME'24 about 65% to 76.7%
NVIDIA Data Flywheel [25][26][27] Elasticsearch docs with workload_id Dedup, stratified split LoRA via NeMo Customizer; ICL LLM judge; tool-call accuracy Human promotion only Up to 98.6% cost reduction (1B vs 70B on tool routing)
Agent Lightning [28][29][30] Gateway proxy recording token IDs and logprobs Merge only on continuous token histories RL (verl), APO, RS-SFT Agent-emitted reward events Trainer endpoints SWE-bench Verified +13.8 to +14.6 pts
RouteLLM / RoRF [31][32] Preference or battle data GPT-4-judge augmentation MF, BERT, LLM classifier, random forest MT Bench, MMLU, GSM8K Threshold router-mf-t Up to 85% cost cut at 95% GPT-4 quality

12. Cross-cutting failure modes

  1. Reward hacking of LLM graders. OpenAI's RFT run gained 20–30 points on a lexical-heavy rubric without improving clinical accuracy [3]. Mitigations: adversarial and contrastive grader examples, down-weighting easily gamed components, validating the grader's ranking before training, and running small pilots first [3]. Agent Lightning ships explicit "reward-hacking prevention" in its coding-agent pipeline [28].
  2. Teacher-as-ground-truth ceilings. When eval labels are the production model's own outputs, a student can at best match the teacher. Systematic teacher errors become invisible [15][25]. Use gold labels on a slice and remove teacher errors, which improved students in the Jigsaw study [15].
  3. Eval/train leakage and moving test sets. Deduplicate across splits and freeze regression sets [15][26].
  4. Task mixing. Without per-node task ids, datasets blend incompatible behaviours [25][26].
  5. Aggregate metrics hide tail failures. "95%" can hide the critical 5% [26]. Manual error analysis (open and axial coding, reviewing individual mistakes) is recommended by OpenAI, Hamel Husain and Predibase alike [5][15].
  6. Hidden cost regressions. Smaller models that think longer or emit more tokens can cancel the savings. The RFT-tuned o4-mini used more reasoning tokens [3][26].
  7. Retokenization and serialization drift in RL from logged text [30].
  8. Non-repeatable environments. GRPO-style RL needs many rollouts per scenario, so it does not suit agents with irreversible side effects. Sandboxes or replayable environments are needed, ideally behind a standard interface such as OpenEnv [12][28][49].
  9. Router calibration drift. Thresholds calibrated on public data do not hold on product traffic, and must be recalibrated on recent queries [31][32].
  10. Privacy and terms of service. NVIDIA's reference flow fine-tunes on traffic without PII removal, and lists redaction as roadmap work [25][26]. OpenTelemetry marks prompt and completion content as opt-in and likely to contain PII [44]. The playbook advises checking provider terms before training on their outputs [15].

Key takeaways for system designers

  • Design the log schema for training on day one. Store the exact request, the exact response and a stable task id per call site, plus model, prompt version and user-feedback fields. For anything that may become RL, also store the token IDs and logprobs from the inference engine [25][29][30]. Prefer an open schema (OpenTelemetry GenAI spans and evaluation events), and remember that message content is opt-in there: turn it on deliberately, with redaction and retention rules [44][45].
  • Decide whether to reuse or regenerate targets. Logged responses are free but frozen at whatever model and prompt were live; re-querying a current teacher on logged prompts costs more but removes stale labels [1][47].
  • Keep logging off the critical path. Use async reporting, stream passthrough and client fallback when the logging service is down [9].
  • Build the evaluator before the trainer. Freeze an in-distribution and a stress or balanced test set. Align LLM judges to SME labels with TPR and TNR, and treat every grader as an adversary the policy will exploit [3][5][15].
  • Pick the cheapest learning signal that works. Prompt and ICL changes come first (the NVIDIA icl arm and GEPA). Then SFT distillation on narrow tasks, then on-policy distillation to fix exposure bias or restore general skills, and RL (RFT, GRPO, RULER) only when outcomes are verifiable and rollouts are repeatable [12][25][39][40].
  • Distill per workload, serve as adapters. Multi-LoRA serving makes per-task and per-tenant specialists affordable, which is what lets the flywheel keep spinning [16][17].
  • Use routers as the promotion mechanism. Ship the student behind a calibrated router, log the escalations, and feed them back as both router training data and new distillation targets [15][31].
  • Automate the search, not the promotion. Every reference system surfaces candidates and leaves the production decision to humans, with versioned rollback [6][25][26].
  • Measure total cost per task, including tokens generated, grader spend and judge latency, not just the per-token price of the model [3][26].
